channel.title: The Brief — Adam's News
channel.description: Every story from Adam's three daily briefs (9 AM / 5 PM / 10 PM CT) as its own item, readable right in your feed reader, with a link to the original article.

item.title: Bridges on both sides: Ukraine collapses the Kerch road span as Russia hits Kyiv's crossings
item.description:
Ukraine severely damaged the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea overnight, collapsing a section of its road span, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called an "unprecedented" operation — while Russia answered by firing seven ballistic missiles at two of Kyiv's main bridges across the Dnipro, killing at least two people in the capital and knocking out power, water and heating. It was the second straight night of record-scale drone warfare on both sides, and it landed on the morning of the Ramstein defence meeting in Brussels and two days before Thursday's Trump–Putin–Xi summit in Shenzhen.
The details, as reported by the Press Association, Reuters and Ukrainian officials: Ukraine's General Staff said an arch and a span of the Kerch Bridge's road section collapsed, severing the road link, while the railway line was still standing but its arch was damaged. Zelensky said the attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes in seven stages — knocking out air defences, radars and electronic-warfare equipment first — before domestically built long-range drones hit the road section and Neptune missiles and other drones targeted the rail section, with Flamingo precision-guided missiles delivering the final blow. Russia's Investigative Committee said the bridge was attacked by drones and sustained damage; Crimea's Moscow-installed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, said traffic was halted but rail traffic was restored by Tuesday afternoon, without mentioning damage. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said there was "no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than it was before." Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences downed 1,441 Ukrainian drones overnight — a day after claiming 1,336, the previous record — and Moscow's mayor said around 800 drones flew toward the capital region, 321 shot down as they approached. Independent outlet Astra reported a huge fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan, nearly 1,300 km from the border.
In Kyiv, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles hit the Southern Bridge and three hit the Northern Bridge. Both were closed to traffic, the metro system was partially damaged, and fires broke out in four districts. Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported two deaths in Kyiv's Obolonskyi district. Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said overnight strikes left consumers without power in eight Ukrainian regions; Zelensky put the figure at significant outages in three regions. Russian strikes also hit Zaporizhzhia, killing two people and wounding 18, and industrial facilities in three districts of the region. The Russian Defence Ministry confirmed strikes on Ukrainian transport, energy, military and port infrastructure.
The two sides are telling very different stories about what this means. Kyiv frames the Kerch strike as a masterstroke against the symbol of Russia's 2014 annexation — the General Staff's statement was blunt: "The symbol of the occupation has cracked." UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, meeting allies at NATO headquarters in Brussels, called it "another example of Ukrainian ingenuity and Ukraine's absolute determination to defend itself." Moscow, for its part, treats the bridge as repairable and the Kyiv strikes as routine — its Defence Ministry described the overnight barrage as a strike on military-industrial, energy, transport and port infrastructure, and Peskov promised a better bridge. Zelensky, meanwhile, said Russia has battered Ukrainian infrastructure, especially the power grid, every day, and that "we have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection." He also said on Monday that Russia is receiving dozens of ballistic missiles from North Korea every month and urged allies to give Ukraine comparable weapons for "missile parity." On diplomacy, the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the US and European partners held a working video call on Monday about the Abu Dhabi talks and next steps; Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, said "we aligned our positions and our next joint steps." The US was represented by envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and the commander of US forces in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich.
For ordinary people, this is now a war on the routes they use every day. In Kyiv, two of the eight bridges across the Dnipro are shut, buses and trolleybuses have been diverted, the metro is partly damaged, and parts of the city are without water, power and heating as winter closes in. In Crimea, the road link that moves military and civilian supplies to the peninsula is severed, at least for now. And in Russia, the drone war is reaching deeper — Bashkortostan is nearly 1,300 km from Ukraine's border. The immediate test is today in Brussels: Germany's Defence Minister Boris Pistorius announced a $300 million contribution to NATO's PURL programme for US weapons for Ukraine — its fifth package — focused on PAC-2 and PAC-3 Patriot missiles, with Germany and Norway sponsoring the package. Patriot missiles are the only weapon reliable enough to stop Russian ballistic missiles, but there is a global shortage, made worse since the US launched its war against Iran. Germany is also working to integrate its IRIS-T missile with Norwegian NASAMS systems and will deliver additional radars, drone ammunition and fighter jets. NATO allies will also discuss Washington's review of US troop levels in Europe with Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, who is attending the Ramstein meeting; more clarity on any drawdown is expected within weeks.
In short: both sides struck the other's bridges overnight — Ukraine collapsed part of the Kerch road span after weeks of preparation, Russia hit Kyiv's North and South bridges with seven ballistic missiles and cut power in eight regions — in the biggest drone exchange of the war so far. Watch today's Ramstein meeting for Patriot missiles, and Thursday's Shenzhen trilateral, where Trump says he will raise Ukraine with Xi and Putin even though US officials say it is not on the agenda.
Sources:
Source: content.assets.pressassociation.io.

item.title: Two more tankers hit in Hormuz as the US and Iran trade blows — and oil falls anyway
item.description:
The Gulf war's sharpest escalation in days came on Sunday night and Monday, with two more tankers confirmed hit in the Strait of Hormuz, a US strike on Iranian missile launchers reported but not confirmed by Washington, a drone alarm at Iraq's biggest gas field, and the Houthis closing in on Aden — yet oil prices fell, not rose, as traders bet on a global supply surplus.
The details, as reported by Reuters and Al Jazeera: the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency confirmed two tanker attacks in the strait on Monday. In the latest, a tanker was disabled and an engine-room fire broke out after an attack seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman; earlier, another tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile while travelling out of the strait, also causing an engine-room fire. No casualties were reported in either. Maritime monitor Vanguard identified the first vessel as the Panama-flagged On Phoenix, hit about three nautical miles off Oman. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy said two oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire while trying to cross the southern part of the strait through a route Tehran considers unauthorised, and Iran's regular navy said another tanker caught fire and was immobilised after hitting a mine east of the strait — bringing the Guard's claimed tally to six tankers on fire since Sunday. None of the Iranian mine claims has been independently verified, and Iranian authorities have not identified the vessels. The Guard also said it seized a US MQ-170 drone near Qeshm Island after an electronic-warfare operation; that claim is also unverified. Euronews reported that the US military launched airstrikes on Iranian missile launchers at Bandar Lengeh and Sirik in southern Iran on Sunday night, after Iranian forces attacked a US base in Bahrain and fired on tankers — but US Central Command has not confirmed the strikes, and other outlets note the report cites no confirming source. Iran did carry out a drone attack on a radar at the US Al Riffa air base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second in three days; Bahrain and Washington say every drone was shot down, with no injuries or damage. The USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the region over the weekend, joining the USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush — three US carrier strike groups in the Middle East for the first time since the Iraq war.
The fighting is also spreading inland. In Iraq's Kurdistan region, warning sirens sounded on Monday after a drone flew over the Khor Mor gas field, Reuters reported, citing two security sources. There were no immediate reports of a strike or damage — but production at Khor Mor had already been halted the previous week after a suspected drone attack sparked a fire and knocked out 2.8 gigawatts of electricity generation, according to Dana Gas, one of the field's operators. The field supplies most of the natural gas for power generation in Iraqi Kurdistan, and Kurdish officials have blamed Iranian-backed armed groups for repeated attacks on it. No group was identified as responsible for Monday's flyover. In Yemen, the Houthis have advanced to about 60 km from Aden after government-aligned forces withdrew from positions overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait to reinforce the city's defence; the Houthis now control the area overlooking the strategic waterway. The International Organization for Migration said at least 348,000 people have been displaced in fighting between Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis since August 1, including 18,780 between November 8 and 14. Saudi Arabia replaced the commander of its coalition forces in Yemen on Monday, appointing General Fayyad al-Ruwaili in place of Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman. The Houthis claimed Saudi forces launched 88 airstrikes and missile attacks in 24 hours against Sanaa and several governorates; those claims have not been independently verified.
The two sides' positions are hardening in opposite directions. Tehran is floating a two-day plan to reopen Hormuz — Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in Muscat on Tuesday after an Economic Cooperation Organisation meeting in Islamabad, said the organisation welcomed the proposal — but it is conditional on Washington accepting Iran's terms, and Tehran has ruled out curbs on uranium enrichment and IAEA access to damaged nuclear sites. Iran also warned vessels against entering areas it considers unauthorised and said ships must coordinate with its armed forces. Washington, for its part, has not confirmed the reported Sunday-night strikes, and Vice President JD Vance said there was no disagreement between him and President Trump over Iran, acknowledging the political cost of higher energy prices but saying the conflict would not become a "forever war." Trump has said further strikes on Iran are "quite unlikely" and that the military part of the war is "effectively over" — even as the fighting widens.
For ordinary people, the disconnect between the battlefield and the market is the story. Brent crude fell to about $91.66–$91.80 a barrel on Tuesday, down roughly 0.8%, with WTI around $85, despite the fresh tanker attacks — the IEA said on Friday that the global oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, with supply running about 1.7 million barrels a day above demand, and Middle East exports recovering faster than demand. Traffic through the strait is still only about 49% of its pre-war level, according to ANZ bank estimates, and marine underwriters have repriced transit exposure to near-prohibitive levels. The human cost is concentrated in Yemen, where more than a third of a million people have been displaced since August, and in Iraqi Kurdistan, where the Khor Mor shutdown has already cut power generation. Iran is also facing warnings of winter gas shortages, with its government forecasting a peak-demand deficit of about 430 million cubic metres per day.
In short: two tankers were confirmed hit in Hormuz on Monday, Iran claims six on fire since Sunday (unverified), the US is reported to have struck missile launchers at Bandar Lengeh and Sirik (unconfirmed by CENTCOM), a drone buzzed Iraq's Khor Mor gas field, and the Houthis are closing on Aden — but oil fell anyway on surplus forecasts. Watch Araghchi's talks in Muscat today, and whether CENTCOM confirms the Sunday-night strikes.
Sources:
Source: aljazeera.com.

item.title: Nvidia's first earnings without Huang land tonight — with the stock down 30% in a month
item.description:
Nvidia reports third-quarter results after the market closes today, its first earnings call since co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12 — and the numbers will land with the stock at its lowest in months and the whole AI rally on trial. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also still CFO, leads the call at 5 p.m. ET, with results expected at about 4:20 p.m. ET.
The details, as reported by USA Today, CoinDesk and market data: consensus is revenue of about $108.7–$109.1 billion and adjusted earnings of about $2.47 a share, against Nvidia's own guidance of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. The quarter ended October 25, before Huang resigned, so the results will show what Nvidia delivered under him; the fourth-quarter outlook from Kress will be the first look at what management expects after the handover, and options imply a swing of roughly 7–9% either way. The stock closed Monday at $156.14, down 4.12% on the day and its lowest close since July 1, 2025, after falling about 12% last week. It was trading around $155.26 in Tuesday morning trade, down about 27.5% over the past month and roughly 30% below its October record high of $243.37, with a market capitalisation of about $3.92 trillion. The Nasdaq fell 2.49% on Monday into a correction, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index lost 5.3%. Reuters, citing anonymous sources, reported that Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back, despite a "Stand with Jensen" petition that has passed 180,000 signatures, including thousands of employees and shareholders. Huang is due to give a closed-door congressional interview before Thanksgiving and testify under oath to the Senate Banking Committee on December 3. Anthropic's IPO, with trading set to start Thursday on Nasdaq at a targeted valuation of about $1.4 trillion, is the other big test of the AI market this week.
The arguments around the company split two ways. The bull case, such as it is, is that the business itself is still growing fast — consensus revenue is up about 91% year on year — and that demand for AI hardware has not gone away. The bear case is about leadership and trust: Huang stepped down amid allegations involving an extramarital relationship and an investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation, and investors are asking what Nvidia is without the founder who built it over 33 years. Some big shareholders, including Altimeter's Brad Gerstner, have urged a slow, deliberate CEO search and keeping a possible Huang return on the table; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for a broader leadership shake-up and an outsider. Reuters also reported on Tuesday that Nvidia has warned customers about legal exposure once the US Remote Access Security Act took effect and stopped supplying buyers who sublease more than half their GPUs to Chinese firms.
For ordinary people, the stakes are mostly in retirement accounts and the broader market: Nvidia is the world's third-largest company and the anchor of the AI rally, so a bad print tonight could drag the Nasdaq further into its correction. Separately, Nvidia announced its Vera CPU rack-scale platform for high-performance computing at the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago on Tuesday — 192 of its first fully custom data-centre CPUs, interconnected by Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking, with more than 200 TB/s of aggregate peak memory bandwidth for climate modelling, molecular dynamics and agentic science. Racks are expected from Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro from early 2027. ASUS and Penguin Solutions also announced Vera Rubin NVL72 rack systems shipping now, with 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs per rack.
In short: tonight's earnings are really two tests — the quarter Huang delivered, and the outlook Kress gives for the company without him. Watch the 4:20 p.m. ET release and the 5 p.m. call, especially the fourth-quarter guidance, and whether the board says anything new about the CEO search.
Sources:
Source: usatoday.com.

item.title: Google Opal shuts down today — your AI apps won't transfer automatically:
item.description:
Google is shutting down its experimental no-code AI app builder Opal on November 17, 2026, without automatically moving existing workflows to Gemini Skills or another platform.
Users can keep saved workflow files in Google Drive, but the service that runs them is going away, so apps that depend on it will need rebuilding. Google says lessons from Opal helped shape Gemini Skills; eligible Gems on adult personal accounts automatically transition to Skills today.
Why it matters: anyone who built automations in Opal has to rebuild them now. (TechRepublic)
Source: techrepublic.com.

item.title: GitHub trending, November 17: REA keeps climbing, Univer and SkillEvaluator rise:
item.description:
morluto/rea is now at about 465,000 stars, up roughly 17,000 in a week; pingdotgg/t3code is at about 63,000; Ebony-Vinyl/dsh-our-free-model at about 78,000; storytold/craft-anything at about 35,000; libracoder/kiri — a small, fast container runtime for macOS, Windows and Linux with a free Ngrok alternative — at about 9,600; dream-num/univer, the open-source office SDK, at about 27,700 after gaining roughly 1,900 in a day; and NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator, a framework for evaluating AI agent skills and plugins with quality gates and synthetic evaluation datasets, at about 3,100.
New on the daily picks: deepseek-ai/chat-demo (about 4,200 stars) and huamidev/GestaltX, a MobileGestalt editor for iOS 27.x. (Daily Diff · FindaRepo · GitDiscover · Trendar)

item.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 flaw CVE-2026-119618: unauthenticated remote code execution, patch now:
item.description:
Apache fixed a critical race condition in mod_http2 in version 2.4.71, released November 11.
The flaw lets an unauthenticated remote attacker corrupt server memory and potentially execute code with the privileges of the Apache process — but only on servers with HTTP/2 enabled; HTTP/1.1-only servers are not exposed. Versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 are affected, as is standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.
Red Hat scores it 9.8; CISA scores it 8.1. A public proof-of-concept showing heap corruption appeared on November 12, but no public RCE exploit and no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and it is not in CISA's KEV catalog.
Notably, the flaw was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner — the free LLM vulnerability scanner for open-source projects — alongside Google Cloud Vulnerability Research. Why it matters: Apache runs a huge share of the web, and HTTP/2 is on by default in many setups; upgrade to 2.4.71 or your distribution's fixed package.
(Wordfence · CIRCL · Sysdig)
Source: wordfence.com.

item.title: Knesset speaker vote today: Kahana set to replace Ohana:
item.description:
Israel's Knesset is voting at 4 p.m. local time on Tuesday to elect a successor to Speaker Amir Ohana, after 67 lawmakers signed a request to put the election on the agenda.
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot has nominated Matan Kahana, a lawmaker from Eisenkot's Yashar party and former religious affairs minister; Likud nominated Ofir Katz, backed by Shas and United Torah Judaism. Kahana was expected to win with support from the Arab parties — the Joint List signalled its backing — completing the opposition's control of key parliamentary positions before government formation.
The vote matters because the speaker chairs debates and decides what reaches the floor. (Asia Today · News in Israel · Jewish Rhode Island)
Source: asiatoday.id.

item.title: Apple to face trial in France over planned obsolescence:
item.description:
Apple will be tried in France in June 2027 to answer accusations that it obstructed iPhone repairs "outside its authorized channels," the association Halte à l'Obsolescence Programmée (HOP) announced on Monday.
HOP filed the complaint four years ago; it calls out "serialization" — parts paired to specific devices. Apple stores currently charge over €400 to replace a screen on the latest-generation iPhone.
Why it matters: a conviction could force Apple to loosen repair restrictions in France and set a precedent across the EU. (Le Monde)
Source: lemonde.fr.

item.title: Russia hit two of Kyiv's bridges late Monday — hours after Trump said Putin is "backing down"
item.description:
Russian forces struck Kyiv's North and South bridges across the Dnipro River late on Monday night, knocking out water and power in parts of the capital, in an overnight barrage that also hit Cherkasy, Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia. The strikes landed hours after President Donald Trump, leaving the White House for Asia, said he thought Vladimir Putin was "backing down a little bit" in Ukraine — and floated a possible meeting with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China, a surprise that would put a fourth leader at the week's summit table.
The details, as reported by Reuters and France 24: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram that, according to preliminary information, there had been hits on the North and South bridges, and later added that parts of the city had water and power cuts. Reuters witnesses reported a series of loud explosions in the capital. A Russian missile attack injured three people in the Cherkasy region, and strikes also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-biggest city, and critical and industrial infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia, local officials said. Reuters said it could not immediately independently confirm the bridge reports. Russia has attacked bridges over the Dnipro earlier this month and in October. The attacks continued overnight, with the Crimea Bridge hit again and Moscow saying it downed nearly 200 drones heading in its direction, according to Telegram statements. President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday that intelligence showed Russia planned strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday — and that Ukraine had held new online talks with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as well as European representatives, on ending the war. Kushner said progress was made toward an agreement, though important challenges remain. The barrage followed Ukraine's record overnight drone attack into Russia on Sunday night, which Moscow said involved 1,336 drones downed across 16 regions.
The diplomacy is where the two sides' stories diverge sharply. Trump told reporters before boarding Air Force One that he thought Putin "is backing down a little bit," adding "I think he'd like to see it finished" and "I think he could be tougher." He also said Ukraine would be discussed at Thursday's trilateral with Xi Jinping and Putin in Shenzhen — scheduled for 2:30 p.m. local time at Shenzhen Kylin Villa, according to Roll Call — along with denuclearization, Iran, trade and the economy. Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said a one-on-one meeting between Trump and Putin in Shenzhen was also being arranged, according to the Associated Press. Then the surprise: asked about Kim, Trump said "We may meet with Kim Jong Un also… He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi." Neither Beijing nor Pyongyang had confirmed anything by the time he spoke, and North Korea has publicly indicated it has no intention of meeting Trump at this time, according to TBS News. A US official said last week there were no plans for North Korea engagement on the trip. The White House and senior US officials have said Ukraine is not on the trilateral agenda and no agreement is expected — a direct contradiction of what Trump said on the tarmac.
For ordinary people in Kyiv, the bridge strikes are a new kind of target: bridges are how the city moves, and hitting two of them at once, on top of the energy campaign, means longer commutes, disrupted water and power, and another night of air-raid alerts. Zelensky warned on Sunday that the ballistic missile threat "remains very serious." In Russia, meanwhile, the drone war is reaching deeper — Moscow's mayor reported around 600 drones aimed at the capital region since Sunday evening.
In short: Russia answered Trump's "backing down" remark with a night of strikes on Kyiv's bridges and three more regions, while the Shenzhen summit keeps growing — a trilateral on Thursday, a possible Trump–Putin one-on-one, and now a floated Kim meeting that nobody has confirmed. Watch Tuesday: Ramstein, and whether the overnight barrage continues as Zelensky's intelligence warned.
Sources:
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Drones hit four ships off Romania — inside NATO waters, and Bucharest is asking allies for help
item.description:
Drones struck four commercial vessels in the Black Sea near Romania's Sulina Canal over Friday and Saturday, two of them inside Romanian territorial waters, in the sharpest escalation yet of the shipping war spilling into NATO territory. Romania has declared the area dangerous to navigation, scrambled fighter jets twice, and is now asking allies for surveillance aircraft and counter-drone equipment.
The details, confirmed by Romania's defence ministry and reported by Reuters: on Saturday evening, the Greek-flagged oil and chemical tanker Evia Petrol V was hit at about 9:10 p.m. local time, roughly four nautical miles east-southeast of Sulina, and a fire broke out on board that the crew extinguished. About 35 minutes later the bulk carrier Marsol was struck about five nautical miles southeast of the Sulina Canal, also catching fire, also put out by its crew. A third vessel, the oil-products tanker Ali Najafov, reported a drone strike near the Danube's mouths the same night. A fourth ship, the Palau-flagged general cargo vessel Larissa 1, was hit on Friday evening. No casualties were reported in any of the four incidents. Romania's Maritime Hydrographic Directorate issued a radio navigational warning on Sunday advising commercial vessels to avoid the area, and the defence ministry said it scrambled F-16s on two occasions after detecting aerial targets, including one near Snake Island. The Sulina Canal is one of the main links between the Danube and the Black Sea and is used by Ukraine for exports — Evia Petrol V had been waiting to enter the canal to load about 6,500 tonnes of sunflower oil.
Bucharest has not formally named who launched the drones, but Prime Minister Luca Niculescu and Defence Minister Stefan-Radu Oprea both called the strikes a direct consequence of Russia's war in Ukraine, and Oprea said they were violations of international law. France has deployed Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft as reinforcement, according to Business Recorder, and Oprea will seek allied surveillance aircraft and counter-drone equipment at a Brussels meeting. Moscow has said nothing about the incidents. The attacks follow a series of incidents involving commercial vessels near the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts through October and November.
For ordinary people, the stakes are food and fuel prices: the Sulina route carries Ukrainian grain and sunflower oil to world markets, and every incident like this raises insurance costs and pushes shippers to reroute. It also puts a NATO member's territorial waters directly in the line of fire — the first time the Black Sea shipping war has hit ships inside a NATO country's waters rather than near them.
In short: four ships hit in two nights, two of them inside Romanian territorial waters, no casualties but fires on board and a navigation warning in force. Bucharest is treating it as part of Russia's war and asking NATO allies for help watching the coast. Watch the Brussels meeting and whether any shipowner or insurer pulls out of the Sulina route.
Sources:
Source: seenews.com.

item.title: Tankers still burning in Hormuz, Houthis 60 km from Aden — and Tehran offers a two-day plan to reopen the strait
item.description:
The Gulf war's 263rd day brought burning tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a Houthi advance to within about 60 kilometres of Aden, and a diplomatic opening from Tehran — a two-day plan to reopen the strait — while Washington signalled it is preparing its forces for a long confrontation rather than an early settlement.
The details, as reported by The Atlantic Digest and Reuters: Iranian state television, as quoted by Bloomberg, put the number of vessels that had caught fire in the strait since Sunday at six, including a supertanker said to be carrying more than two million barrels of crude. None of the Iranian mine claims has been independently verified, and the Guard has warned oil companies the southern route is mined. The one incident a neutral agency has confirmed remains the UK Maritime Trade Operations report from Monday morning of a tanker hit by an unknown projectile near Oman, causing an engine-room fire with no casualties. A tracker cited by Dawn estimated crude flows through Hormuz had fallen to about eight million barrels a day by November 15, roughly 47 percent of the pre-war level — though oil still fell on Monday, with Brent settling at $92.44, down $3.40 (3.6%), and WTI at $85.72, down $2.84 (3.2%), on recovering flows and the IEA's surplus forecast. In Yemen, the Houthis advanced to about 60 km from Aden, military and government sources told AFP, seizing the Al-Maqatirah and Al-Madaribah districts of Lahj province; Reuters reported Houthi fighters had seized ground on the southern coast and that Aden residents described new checkpoints and identity checks. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two Houthi drones launched toward the Mecca and Riyadh regions, and Saudi Arabia replaced the coalition's commander, Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman, with General Fayyad al-Ruwaili. Late on Monday, the Iranian agency Mehr, quoted by Reuters, reported air defences had been activated in Isfahan, with no cause given.
Tehran's message on diplomacy was mixed. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spent Monday in Islamabad at an Economic Cooperation Organisation meeting, saying it had responded positively to an Iranian proposal he described as a two-day plan for the Strait of Hormuz, and that members hoped it would lead to a definitive and comprehensive ceasefire — though Dawn reported the plan is conditional on Washington accepting Iran's terms. Araghchi is due in Muscat on Tuesday for talks with his Omani counterpart. But parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the path to ending the conflict stayed open only if Washington accepted what he called Iran's logical conditions, foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei ruled out curbs on uranium enrichment as a route to a deal, and deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tehran would not wait for the United States to attack first and that IAEA inspectors would not get access to damaged nuclear sites until Iran's conditions were met. Washington's posture points the same way: the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group entered Central Command waters on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington — Bloomberg noted the US last had three carrier groups in the region in 2003 — and the Army is seeking contractors to build 17 reinforced-concrete bunkers to protect troops in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon, calling the requirement urgent and high priority, with completion within 45 days of a task order. Iranian missiles and drones have killed at least 23 American personnel in the region, according to Military Times, including six in a strike on an Army command post in Kuwait in March. Trump said Iran would be discussed at this week's Shenzhen summit and that "we have Iran in very good shape," while the New York Times reported the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran's energy infrastructure.
For ordinary people, the disconnect between the battlefield and the market is the story: despite burning tankers and a supertanker said to have sunk, fuel prices are falling, not rising, because flows are recovering faster than feared. The human cost is concentrated in Yemen, where the Houthi advance toward Aden has displaced hundreds of thousands and blocked aid, and in Bahrain, where a court on Monday sentenced 64 people to between 15 years and life in prison on charges of forming a group linked to the Revolutionary Guard, according to ABC News.
In short: the shipping war is still escalating — six tankers claimed hit since Sunday, the Houthis closing on Aden — but Tehran is also floating a two-day plan to reopen Hormuz, and Washington is digging in for a long fight, with three carriers on station and emergency bunkers going up. Watch Tuesday's Araghchi talks in Muscat, and whether any maritime agency confirms mines in the southern lanes.
Sources:
Source: atlanticdigest.com.

item.title: French troops reported operating inside Ukraine:
item.description:

item.title: Nvidia closed at its lowest since July 2025 — the day before its first earnings without Huang
item.description:
Nvidia shares closed Monday at $156.14, down $6.71 or 4.12%, the company's lowest close since July 1, 2025, according to CNN — after falling about 12% last week and now down nearly 24% this month. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index lost 5.3%, and Intel and Micron each fell more than 7%. The broader market slid with it: the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.49% to 24,509.76, in a correction by the wire's measure, the S&P 500 fell 1.92% to 7,416.59, and the Dow fell 739 points, or 1.41%, to 51,608.17. The petition urging Huang's reinstatement has passed 180,000 signatures, but the board was reported on Monday not to be discussing his return. Nvidia reports third-quarter results Tuesday at about 4:20 p.m. ET, with the earnings call at 5 p.m. ET — the first report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, presented by interim CEO Colette Kress. Consensus is revenue of about $109.1 billion and adjusted EPS of $2.47. The quarter itself ended October 25, before Huang's departure, so the numbers will show what Nvidia delivered under him; the fourth-quarter outlook will be the first look at what management expects after the handover. Also on the week's calendar: Anthropic's IPO, with trading set to start Thursday on Nasdaq and the company targeting a valuation of about $1.4 trillion.
Sources:
Source: eurasiabusinessnews.com.

item.title: Apple: iOS 27.3 beta 2 adds face unlock for the Duo — and Siri starts answering health questions
item.description:
Apple seeded the second beta of iOS 27.3 on Monday. The headline change for the iPhone Duo is a front-camera face unlock option, usable only when the phone is closed and only on the Lock Screen — a partial answer to the most common complaint about the foldable, which shipped without Face ID. The beta also lets Siri AI answer questions about your health data (step counts, heart rate, Activity rings) and log medications, and adds an "Ask About Page" feature that lets Siri read a whole Safari page. macOS 27.3 beta 2 (Golden Gate) adds vertical tabs in Safari and native Live Activities. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Corey Fugman, a 26-year Apple veteran, will take over Apple Pay, Wallet and Apple Card from the retiring Jennifer Bailey. Apple has promised iOS 27.3 for December.
Sources:
Source: macrumors.com.

item.title: Air-raid alert apps in both Russia and Ukraine were hacked — fake nuclear warnings sent to phones
item.description:
Ukraine's air-raid alert app was hacked on Sunday evening, sending users fake warnings of nuclear and chemical threats around Kyiv, warnings of street combat, and a false claim that Russia's hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed. The Ukrainian Air Force said on Telegram: "The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence. There is no radiation threat!" Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications blamed Russia. Hours later, early on Monday morning, Russia's Emergencies Ministry said its own warnings app came under a "massive cyberattack" that spread false information about incoming drone attacks. The announcements followed the end of a localized truce in part of Russian-occupied Kherson region on Sunday — the longest of the war so far. The Kyiv-specific alert app kept working normally, according to Kyiv authorities. For anyone relying on these apps, the lesson is the same as with any emergency channel: a single app is a single point of failure, and official Telegram channels were the fallback both sides pointed to.
Sources:
Source: aljazeeranews-3fuh52rgrl.edgeone.app.

item.title: Russell Brand: foreign secretary calls his prison message "revolting" — and nearly 400 creatives sign a letter against a "culture of silence"
item.description:
The fallout from Russell Brand's prison message kept growing on Monday. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News the crimes were "heinous and awful" and called it "revolting" that Brand showed no remorse in the message his wife read out on YouTube on Sunday — in which Brand said "I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening." Miliband also apologised for appearing on Brand's online show in 2015. The Ministry of Justice is urgently investigating whether the message breached prison rules, which bar prisoners from making statements that cause distress to victims, and Downing Street called it "clearly appalling." Separately, nearly 400 British creatives — including Natalie Dormer — signed an open letter demanding stronger protections for people who report misconduct in entertainment and accountability for those who help conceal abuse, organised after Brand's convictions and the publication of allegations against David Walliams. The Metropolitan Police launched an investigation on November 13 into separate allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s. Brand was sentenced on November 9 to 10 years and six months for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault; no appeal has been filed, with the windows running to December 3 for conviction and December 7 for sentence.
Sources:
Source: worldrightnowlive.com.

item.title: Russia could fire 6,500 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in November — and the strikes are already intensifying
item.description:
Russia could launch up to 6,500 jet-powered Shahed-type drones at Ukraine in November, a twelvefold increase from about 530 in August, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Monday in an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. The warning landed on a day when Russian strikes kept hitting Ukrainian energy and industry, the EU hit Moscow with fresh sanctions, and Kyiv heads into a pivotal week of defence talks — while the question of whether Ukraine will even be discussed at Thursday's Trump–Putin–Xi summit in Shenzhen is still unresolved.
The details, as reported by RFE/RL and the Associated Press: the jet-powered Shaheds are faster and harder to intercept than the older propeller-driven drones, and Ukraine intercepted only about 55% of the 2,730 jet-powered drones Russia launched in September, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky. Koretskyi said the 6,500 estimate is based on the current pace of attacks, and that the government is working to protect energy facilities and equip critical infrastructure with backup power while preparing to repair what cannot be protected. On Monday alone, Russia launched 158 long-range drones at Ukraine, 77 of them jet-powered, causing outages in six regions. A Russian strike on Dnipro killed at least one person and injured three, another hit a critical industrial facility in the Vinnytsia region, and drone attacks on energy facilities in Cherkasy left consumers without power. Ukraine's first deputy energy minister, Artem Nekrasov, said Russia carried out 116 deliberate attacks on Ukraine's energy and oil-and-gas sectors in the past week, with 161 incidents damaging infrastructure — down from 128 attacks and 219 incidents the week before, but still leaving hundreds of thousands without electricity in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk on Monday. Zelensky said Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles in the past week.
The diplomacy is moving in parallel. The EU imposed sanctions on Monday on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, plus businesspeople linked to the energy sector and the oil trade, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said of the peace talks: "We do not see that at the moment. We see that Russia is already escalating." Kyiv's priorities this week are the Ramstein Group meeting in Brussels on Tuesday — led by the German and British defence ministers, with Ukraine pressing for more Patriots and NASAMS — and a Coalition of the Willing gathering in Berlin, where Chancellor Friedrich Merz said more than 20 heads of state and government are expected to agree funding for Ukraine's defence in 2027 and a unified position for peace talks. Zelensky called the Berlin meeting one that "could be historic." Meanwhile the Shenzhen summit is now confirmed by all three sides: China confirmed on Monday that Trump, Putin and Xi will meet on Thursday, after Washington and Moscow had already announced it. But the agenda is openly disputed — US officials say Ukraine is not on the trilateral agenda and no agreement is expected, while Trump told reporters on Monday before leaving for Asia that Ukraine was one of the subjects he intends to discuss with Xi and Putin. The White House says the meeting will focus on nuclear arms reduction and Iran; the Kremlin has signalled Putin wants to discuss a Ukraine settlement.
Each side is telling a different story about where this is heading. Kyiv's argument is that the refinery and long-range drone campaign is a justified response to Russia's refusal to de-escalate and its strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure — Zelensky has said Ukraine disabled more than 55% of Russia's refining capacity, a figure Reuters could not independently verify. Moscow's argument is that its defences absorbed the biggest Ukrainian drone attack of the war overnight into Monday — 1,336 drones claimed downed — and that the campaign changes nothing. Washington's position is split in public: Trump has called the refinery strikes "a disgrace," while his envoys say further talks between Moscow's and Kyiv's delegations are expected, with no date announced.
For ordinary people, the war is now measured in blackouts and heating as winter approaches. The International Energy Agency warned Ukraine could face electricity shortages this winter depending on the intensity of attacks and the weather, and noted that more than 30% of Ukrainian households rely on district heating — so power cuts push families toward electric heaters and higher demand. In Russia, fuel shortages have returned to at least half a dozen regions. Zelensky warned on Sunday that the Russian ballistic missile threat "remains very serious" and that intelligence shows new strikes are being prepared.
In short: Russia's jet-drone campaign is scaling up sharply — potentially 6,500 in November — while Ukraine heads into Tuesday's Ramstein meeting and a Berlin summit of allies asking for more air defences, and Thursday's Shenzhen trilateral is confirmed but still unclear on whether Ukraine will even be discussed.
Sources:
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Iran claims the southern Hormuz lanes are "fully mined" — but nobody has confirmed it, and oil fell anyway
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy is now reported to be saying the southern shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz — the ones along the Omani coast that the United States has said are safe and open — are closed and fully mined. The claim, relayed by Saudi outlet Asharq News and picked up by CBS News on Monday afternoon, has not been confirmed by anyone: the Guard itself has issued no statement echoing it, no maritime agency has verified mines in those lanes, and no shipowner has confirmed a halt in traffic. Markets treated it as unconfirmed — Brent crude fell nearly 3% on Monday — but the claim adds a new layer of menace to a shipping war that already has tankers burning.
The details: earlier on Monday, the Guard claimed six tankers had hit mines since Sunday, up from earlier counts, and Iranian state media said two tankers struck mines on Monday leading to explosions — but as before, no vessel names, flags or casualty figures were given, and the claims could not be independently verified. The one incident a neutral agency has confirmed is the UK Maritime Trade Operations report from Monday morning of a tanker hit by an unknown projectile near Oman, causing an engine-room fire with no casualties — already reported in the morning brief. In Yemen, Saudi Arabia's military coalition said it intercepted two Houthi drones launched toward the Mecca and Riyadh regions on Monday. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi travelled from Islamabad to Muscat on Monday as mediation efforts continued, and in Jerusalem, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned during a meeting with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš that "Iran's missiles, its terrorism and its nuclear ambitions do not stop at Israel's borders. Europe is not watching from the sidelines. Europe is a target."
Tehran's argument, as stated by its officials, is that vessels sailing with tracking switched off on unauthorised routes are fair game, and that the blockade is a direct threat to its economy and sovereignty. Washington's position, as framed by US officials and the IEA, is that the economic squeeze is working: Middle East exports through Hormuz have largely recovered to pre-war levels, and the IEA said on Friday the world oil market will return to surplus in the fourth quarter — about 1.7 million barrels a day — as exports recover faster than demand. The US has also said its forces cleared mines from the main shipping routes, and three carrier strike groups are now in the region.
For ordinary people, the disconnect between the claims and the market is the story: despite the mine claims and the tanker fires, Brent fell $2.76 to $93.08 a barrel by midday Monday and WTI dropped to $86.15, with Goldman Sachs forecasting Brent averaging $88 next year and slipping to $78 by December 2027. That means cheaper fuel at the pump in the near term — unless a confirmed mine strike or a halt in traffic changes the picture. The thing to watch is a statement from UKMTO, US Central Command or a ship operator confirming or denying mines in the southern lanes.
In short: Iran is now reported to claim the southern Hormuz lanes are fully mined, but the Guard has issued no statement of its own, no agency has confirmed it, and oil prices fell on recovering flows — treat it as a claim by one side in a war until a maritime agency, the US Navy or a shipowner confirms it.
Sources:
Source: bugoutguide.com.

In short: Iran is now reported to claim the southern Hormuz lanes are fully mined, but the Guard has issued no statement of its own, no agency has confirmed it, and oil prices fell on recovering flows — treat it as a claim by one side in a war until a maritime agency, the US Navy or a shipowner confirms it.

item.title: Nvidia slides again into earnings — petition to bring Huang back passes 170,000
item.description:
Nvidia shares were down about 4% in premarket trading on Monday after falling 12% last week, leaving the stock more than 30% below its recent record highs, ahead of Tuesday's earnings — the first without Jensen Huang. The petition urging Huang's reinstatement has passed 170,000 signatures, including top tech executives, employees and shareholders, according to TipRanks. Wall Street expects adjusted EPS of $2.47 on revenue of about $108.9 billion, up 91% year over year. Also hanging over the week: Anthropic's IPO, which Reuters says will test whether the AI-fuelled bull market still has further to run after Huang's shock exit.

item.title: Barracuda breached through a vendor key nobody retired — and AI agents are now hunting for AI keys
item.description:
Barracuda Networks says an attacker got into about 10 of its cloud accounts over 44 hours on November 1–2, and the company spotted it on November 4. The way in was a cloud access key Barracuda had given an AI company for an earlier project: the project ended, the key stayed live, and it ended up in a config file in that vendor's GitHub repository, where the attacker apparently found it in October. Barracuda put it bluntly: "We did not retire the key when the vendor ... finished that work. That is on us." From there the attacker chained credentials through Barracuda's data analytics setup, source code repositories and Kubernetes clusters, hunting for cryptocurrency secrets like private keys and seed phrases, trying to keep access with a container that mounted the host's file system, and trying to create a new cloud admin account, which was blocked. Barracuda matched the attacker's labels, probing and hunting routines to ARTEX, the open-source AI pentesting tool the FBI warned about last week. The attacker reached a system holding customer integration credentials for Barracuda XDR; Barracuda found no sign those were taken but asked some customers to replace them anyway. If you run anything with vendor keys: pull a list of every cloud access key and service account, and disable anything tied to a vendor, contractor or project that has finished.
The same tooling is showing up at scale. Amazon's threat intelligence team ran decoy servers pretending to be popular LLM services, and found attacker-run AI agents — assessed with moderate confidence to be running on ARTEX, operated by separate China-linked groups — hunting for internet-facing AI gateways and app builders to steal the AI provider keys inside them. Targets included One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, LiteLLM, Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat and Ollama, using default admin credentials like LiteLLM's default master key, half-finished installs anyone could claim, admin pages with no login, and secrets left in JavaScript and environment files. Stolen keys were tested and pooled, then used to run the models doing the searching. Google's Threat Intelligence Group published a related report the same day, saying attackers are running multi-agent frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI during live intrusions, and using LLMs to compare patched and unpatched code to turn a fix into a working exploit faster. Google expects simple, mostly automated attacks within about three months. The practical takeaway for anyone running AI gateways: get admin and API pages off the open internet, change default keys, finish or delete half-done installs, and rotate provider keys.
Sources:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: CVE-2026-99288 (NoisyTCP): remote Linux kernel crash, no login needed
item.description:
Researcher Hyunwoo Kim disclosed NoisyTCP, an 11-year-old bug in the Linux kernel's TCP code. An unauthenticated attacker can send crafted TCP traffic that races SYN cookie handling against socket hashing and ends in a kernel panic — a denial of service, no code execution and no data changes. It hits nearly every distro and works against machines running Nginx, Apache or an SSH server with default settings. The fix was merged into mainline about two weeks ago; Red Hat rates it Important with a draft CVSS of 7.5. No reports of it being used in attacks yet. Watch your distro's security tracker for the kernel update that names CVE-2026-99288, install it and reboot — public-facing web and SSH servers first.
Sources:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: Log4Shell is still opening doors — this time on an old vCenter server
item.description:
Kaspersky's ICS CERT team wrote up a months-long intrusion at a Russian software developer by a group it assesses as Ukrainian. The attackers came in through an exposed SSH service, then broke into a VMware vCenter 7.0.3 server still vulnerable to Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, CVSS 10.0). That gave them root, then the hypervisors, GitLab, Ansible, the domain controller and finally the server used to sign the company's software builds. They hid a backdoor in /etc/cron.hourly/ under the name "pgcache". The target and the politics are far from home, but the path is not: an unpatched vCenter and the same admin password reused across domains. vCenter 7.0 left general support in 2025 — if you're still on it, plan the move to 8.x.
Sources:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: Russell Brand: Downing Street calls his prison message "clearly appalling" — Ministry of Justice investigating
item.description:
Downing Street said on Monday that Russell Brand's prison message — read out by his wife Laura Gallacher on the couple's YouTube programme on Sunday, in which Brand said "I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening" — was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated as a possible breach of prison rules, which bar prisoners from making statements that cause distress to victims. No finding has been announced. Separately, Justice Secretary Alex Norris urged the Bar Standards Board on Monday to address the use of rape myths by defence barristers, following criticism of arguments in Brand's trial — barristers who use rape myths could face practice bans — and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy is meeting leading figures from media, arts and sport today to press for protections for young staff and freelancers against harassment. Brand was sentenced on November 9 to 10 years and six months for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault; no appeal has been filed, with the windows running to December 3 for conviction and December 7 for sentence.
Sources:
Source: objectivedailynews.com.

item.title: Ukraine launches its biggest drone attack of the war — and hits the Crimean Bridge
item.description:
Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia to annexed Crimea overnight into Monday as part of what Russian defence ministry data showed was the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the full-scale war began in 2022 — 1,336 drones claimed downed across 16 regions, surpassing the previous record of 1,254 on October 29. The Kremlin called the bridge damage minor, but the barrage, aimed at Moscow, refineries and the peninsula's lifeline, shows Kyiv's long-range campaign is still escalating days before a Trump–Putin–Xi meeting in Shenzhen.
The details, as reported by Reuters and AFP on Monday morning: Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said around 600 drones were launched at the Moscow region alone, 191 of them brought down. Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-installed governor of Crimea, confirmed on Telegram that "the enemy has hit the Crimea bridge," with road traffic restricted until around midday and an emergency headquarters set up in Kerch. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later said the damage was minor and traffic was continuing; Russia's transport ministry said rail traffic kept running as normal, though four trains to and from the peninsula were delayed. AFP reported the strike appeared to cause only minor damage, while the Ukrainian monitoring channel Crimean Wind claimed an impact on one of the arches of the navigable section — neither account independently verified.
The refinery campaign continued alongside it. Fires broke out at four industrial sites in Azov in the Rostov region, and at an industrial facility in Ilsky in the Krasnodar region — home to an oil refinery — where falling drone debris injured six people, including children. One person was killed in Taganrog. President Volodymyr Zelensky said late Sunday that Ukrainian strikes had knocked out more than 55% of Russia's refining capacity; Reuters could not independently verify that figure, but two industry sources told Reuters last week the renewed attacks had cut refining capacity by about 30%, and Russian officials said fuel shortages had returned to at least half a dozen regions, though without a repeat of the summer's hours-long queues at filling stations.
Russia kept hitting Ukraine overnight too. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 158 drones, 77 of them jet-powered, into the country on Sunday night into Monday morning; defenders downed or suppressed 131, with impacts at 19 locations. Russian strikes hit energy, industrial and transport infrastructure in Vinnytsia, Kyiv, Cherkasy, Odesa, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, with fires at several sites. Russia's defence ministry separately said it struck a cargo ship in the Black Sea that it claimed was carrying military cargo for Ukraine.
Each side is telling a different story about what the exchange means. Kyiv's argument, implicit in the scale of the operation, is that hitting refineries and the bridge degrades Russia's war machine and gives Ukraine leverage — Zelensky has framed the refinery campaign as the pressure that makes Moscow negotiate. Moscow's argument is that its air defences absorbed the biggest attack of the war, the bridge damage was minor, and the campaign changes nothing on a front line that has stayed largely static for months; Putin has previously vowed retaliation "twice over" for refinery strikes. Washington's position is more complicated: Trump has publicly called the refinery strikes "a disgrace," and US officials have said the Ukraine war is not expected to be a focus of this week's Shenzhen meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping. UN Secretary-General António Guterres, speaking at the ASEAN summit in Manila, called for an immediate ceasefire while acknowledging it was hard to be optimistic.
For ordinary people, the war of attrition is now measured in fuel queues and blackouts on both sides. Russian motorists in at least six regions are facing fuel shortages again; in Ukraine, energy and transport sites were hit across seven regions overnight, and Kyiv heads into Tuesday's Ramstein meeting pressing allies over the Starshield speed cap on its drones and air-defence supplies. The Abu Dhabi talks last week — the first direct peace talks in nine months — agreed a major prisoner exchange but produced no breakthrough on territory, and Russia still holds about a fifth of Ukrainian land.
In short: Ukraine's biggest drone barrage of the war hit the Crimean Bridge and set refineries burning, Moscow says its defences held and the damage was minor, and both sides are still escalating while diplomacy stalls ahead of the Shenzhen summit and Tuesday's Ramstein meeting.
Sources:
Source: yallayou.com.

item.title: Hormuz mine campaign widens: three more tankers hit, Iran bars nuclear inspectors, third US carrier on station
item.description:
The Strait of Hormuz mine campaign escalated again overnight. Iran's state TV said on Monday that three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the strait, and the Revolutionary Guards' navy said mines have damaged six tankers since Sunday, with pollution now affecting the strait's coastlines. A British maritime monitor independently confirmed a separate projectile strike on a tanker on Monday morning. Meanwhile Tehran said it will not let UN nuclear inspectors visit war-damaged sites until the conflict ends, and the US now has three aircraft carrier strike groups in the region.
The details: Iran's state TV report, quoting the Guards' navy and the army, warned shipping companies that a US-supported route through the strait remains dangerous because of mines. It gave no vessel names, flags or casualty figures, and no shipowner or flag state had confirmed the sinkings or fires by Monday morning. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said a tanker was hit by an unknown projectile while sailing out of the strait at about 05:58 GMT on Monday, causing an engine-room fire; no injuries were reported. The vessel was identified in other reporting as the Panama-flagged On Phoenix. A third tanker reported being approached by a skiff carrying four armed people about 430 nautical miles east of Socotra. The New York Times reported that the US and Israel have drawn up plans for possible renewed strikes on Iran's economic infrastructure, and the USS Theodore Roosevelt entered Central Command waters on Sunday, joining the George H.W. Bush and George Washington already on station.
Tehran's tone hardened on two fronts. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran "will not wait for the US to attack first" and that UN inspectors will not be allowed into facilities damaged in the war until the conflict ends. That follows Sunday's statement from Iran's parliament speaker that if Washington "makes another mistake," Iran's armed forces will determine "the geography of the battlefield." In Yemen, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of two strikes on Monday that killed three people, including a child — a drone strike on a house in Sanaa's al-Sarar quarter that wounded seven, and airstrikes on a fuel station in Harf Sufian, north of the capital, that killed two and wounded eight. Riyadh made no immediate comment. Israel's military said it struck a weapons shipment from Syria intended for Hezbollah near Janta in northeastern Lebanon — the first time in months it has said it struck deep inside Lebanon. And in Bahrain, a court sentenced 64 Shiite clerics to life imprisonment over an alleged IRGC-linked plot, with rights groups alleging torture and due-process violations in the mass trial.
Each side's argument is now openly stated. Tehran says vessels sailing with tracking switched off on unauthorised routes are fair game, that the blockade is a direct threat to its economy and sovereignty, and that it will not wait to be attacked. Washington's position, as framed by CNN over the weekend, is that the economic squeeze is working — Gulf oil exports are recovering, prices have fallen from their peaks, and Iran has been unable to export meaningful amounts of its own crude for more than two months — so time is on America's side. Riyadh and its coalition partners say the Houthi attacks are indiscriminate, aimed at airports, holy sites and civilian infrastructure, and that their interceptions are defensive. The Gulf states have asked Trump to hold off broader strikes on Iran.
For ordinary people, the shipping war is now a daily fact across the Gulf: crews transit one of the world's most important oil chokepoints under threat of mines, Saudi airports remain disrupted, and in Yemen about 330,000 people have been displaced by the renewed fighting. Brent crude settled Friday at $95.84 a barrel; Monday's claims had not yet been priced in when the brief was written.
In short: Iran claims three more tankers hit mines and says it won't wait to be attacked first, while a British monitor confirmed a real projectile strike on a tanker, the US now has three carriers in the region, and Tehran is shutting UN inspectors out of its damaged nuclear sites — the standoff is tightening, not easing.
Sources:
Source: s.hdnux.com.

A British maritime monitor independently confirmed a separate projectile strike on a tanker on Monday morning. Meanwhile Tehran said it will not let UN nuclear inspectors visit war-damaged sites until the conflict ends, and the US now has three aircraft carrier strike groups in the region.

The details: Iran's state TV report, quoting the Guards' navy and the army, warned shipping companies that a US-supported route through the strait remains dangerous because of mines. It gave no vessel names, flags or casualty figures, and no shipowner or flag state had confirmed the sinkings or fires by Monday morning. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said a tanker was hit by an unknown projectile while sailing out of the strait at about 05:58 GMT on Monday, causing an engine-room fire; no injuries were reported. The vessel was identified in other reporting as the Panama-flagged On Phoenix. A third tanker reported being approached by a skiff carrying four armed people about 430 nautical miles east of Socotra. The New York Times reported that the US and Israel have drawn up plans for possible renewed strikes on Iran's economic infrastructure, and the USS Theodore Roosevelt entered Central Command waters on Sunday, joining the George H.W. Bush and George Washington already on station.

Tehran's tone hardened on two fronts. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran "will not wait for the US to attack first" and that UN inspectors will not be allowed into facilities damaged in the war until the conflict ends. That follows Sunday's statement from Iran's parliament speaker that if Washington "makes another mistake," Iran's armed forces will determine "the geography of the battlefield." In Yemen, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of two strikes on Monday that killed three people, including a child — a drone strike on a house in Sanaa's al-Sarar quarter that wounded seven, and airstrikes on a fuel station in Harf Sufian, north of the capital, that killed two and wounded eight. Riyadh made no immediate comment. Israel's military said it struck a weapons shipment from Syria intended for Hezbollah near Janta in northeastern Lebanon — the first time in months it has said it struck deep inside Lebanon. And in Bahrain, a court sentenced 64 Shiite clerics to life imprisonment over an alleged IRGC-linked plot, with rights groups alleging torture and due-process violations in the mass trial.

Each side's argument is now openly stated. Tehran says vessels sailing with tracking switched off on unauthorised routes are fair game, that the blockade is a direct threat to its economy and sovereignty, and that it will not wait to be attacked. Washington's position, as framed by CNN over the weekend, is that the economic squeeze is working — Gulf oil exports are recovering, prices have fallen from their peaks, and Iran has been unable to export meaningful amounts of its own crude for more than two months — so time is on America's side. Riyadh and its coalition partners say the Houthi attacks are indiscriminate, aimed at airports, holy sites and civilian infrastructure, and that their interceptions are defensive. The Gulf states have asked Trump to hold off broader strikes on Iran.

For ordinary people, the shipping war is now a daily fact across the Gulf: crews transit one of the world's most important oil chokepoints under threat of mines, Saudi airports remain disrupted, and in Yemen about 330,000 people have been displaced by the renewed fighting. Brent crude settled Friday at $95.84 a barrel; Monday's claims had not yet been priced in when the brief was written.

In short: Iran claims three more tankers hit mines and says it won't wait to be attacked first, while a British monitor confirmed a real projectile strike on a tanker, the US now has three carriers in the region, and Tehran is shutting UN inspectors out of its damaged nuclear sites — the standoff is tightening, not easing.

item.title: Nvidia: the comeback talk is real, the board isn't buying it yet — and earnings land Tuesday
item.description:
The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Jensen Huang has discussed returning as Nvidia chief executive with close allies, who have formed a war room to lobby the board and seek White House support. The report landed days after Huang stepped down, and it is now the central question hanging over the company's first earnings report without him, due Tuesday after the market closes.
The details: the FT report, citing people familiar with the matter, is unconfirmed — Nvidia has not commented. The "Stand With Jensen" petition passed 160,000 signatures over the weekend, including more than 7,500 people identifying as Nvidia employees. Prediction markets are unconvinced: Kalshi traders put Huang's return at about 17%, up from 9% on Saturday, behind Arm's Rene Haas at 24% and Nvidia's Ian Buck at 19%. On the other side, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to hire an external CEO and demanded a response within 10 days on whether seemingly unlawful China sales boosted revenue. Interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also staying on as CFO — has cut the company's data-centre guarantee to OpenAI from $250 billion to about $105 billion, according to Dolphin Research.
The numbers tell the other half of the story. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday at about 4:20 p.m. ET, with a call at 5 p.m. Analysts expect about $108.7 billion in revenue, just above the company's own $108 billion forecast, and the options market implies a move of about 7% either way — roughly $270 billion of market value. The quarter ended October 25, before the report that US intelligence suspected Huang's wife Alice of gathering information for Beijing and before Huang's departure, so the headline numbers will probably be fine; what matters is the fourth-quarter forecast, where analysts expect about $124.9 billion, and whether the board gives any signal on the CEO search. Shares closed Friday at $162.85, down about 33% from the October peak, with the market cap down to roughly $3.9 trillion from about $5.8 trillion in early October.
Each side's argument is stark. Huang's supporters — including Elon Musk, Epic's Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator's Garry Tan — say the company lost its soul when he left and only he can run it. The sceptics — SkyBridge's Anthony Scaramucci, analyst Dan Ives and Bessent — say this is not a scandal a board can wave through: an FBI counterintelligence review, DOJ chip-smuggling probes, a Wachtell investigation and a relationship with a direct report mean no board can reinstate a CEO it is still investigating. Trump has suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job.
For ordinary people, the saga matters well beyond Nvidia shareholders: the company's chips power most of the world's AI infrastructure, its spending commitments shape the data-centre buildout, and its stock sits in countless pension funds and 401(k)s. A 7% earnings move either way on Tuesday would be one of the largest single-day swings in market history in dollar terms.
In short: Huang is talking about a comeback and his allies are lobbying hard, but the board, the White House and the prediction markets all say it probably won't happen — and Tuesday's earnings, the first without him, will be judged on the forecast and the CEO search, not the quarter's numbers.
Sources:
Source: longbridge.com.

item.title: Apple: Health AI research study launches
item.description:
Apple announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study on November 15, a virtual research study run with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals. It will evaluate how people trust, understand and actually use conversational health AI tools, with the aim of informing how Apple designs health AI features. The study is open to up to 200,000 eligible participants aged 21 and older across the United States. First features in scope are real-time translation, writing tools and photo cleanup — Siri AI is not included. This is a research study, not a product launch.
Sources:
Source: apple.com.

item.title: Google: November Pixel Drop rolls out — Gemini Intelligence on Pixel 10, Pixel Tag tracker
item.description:
Google's November Pixel Drop started rolling out today, reaching Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 phones first. The headline piece is Gemini Intelligence on Pixel 10, which takes on multi-step tasks — its Rambler voice-typing upgrade strips filler words from dictated messages and formats them into clean text. Call Screen on Pixel 11 now lets Gemini question unknown callers more conversationally, Pixel Search reaches back to Pixel 6, and the new Pixel Tag tracker ($29.99, or $99.99 for a four-pack) is on sale. Google Fi also gets a "super network" that switches eligible Pixels between two of America's top 5G networks and millions of secure Wi-Fi networks, and Fi is cutting select unlimited plans in half for 12 months — that offer ends December 1.
Sources:
Source: the-gadgeteer.com.

item.title: Six unpatched flaws in Danfoss fridge controllers allow remote takeover — the supermarket hack has a root cause
item.description:
Six critical vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controller let remote attackers take unauthorized control of the hardware without any login, according to Dutch security firm Midnight Blue, reporting via The Hacker News. The flaws persist in the latest firmware, 5.4.0, released in November — researchers note the firmware was likely built October 29, before the second wave of attacks and before their vulnerability reports. Government cybersecurity agencies in Germany, Belgium and Ireland have advised operators to disconnect the controllers' management interfaces from the public internet entirely. This is the same controller family behind the October supermarket refrigeration attacks across Europe, where controllers were forced into defrost and freezer temperatures reportedly hit 50°C. If you run AK-SM800A controllers, get their management interfaces off the internet now — there is no patch yet.
Sources:
Source: gazewire.com.

item.title: Coles investigating cyber incident; no evidence of data theft so far
item.description:
Australian supermarket giant Coles told the ASX on Monday, November 16, that it is investigating a cybersecurity incident, working with the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts. The company has not said what kind of incident it is, when it was detected, or which systems are involved. "Based on the findings of our investigation to date, we have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed," Coles said. Stores and online shopping are operating normally; the only disruption identified is a small number of Liquorland click-and-collect orders. The disclosure comes two weeks after the European supermarket refrigeration attacks — no link has been suggested.
Sources:

item.title: Check Point PHP2Shell flaws exploited in the wild since late October
item.description:
Check Point Research documented attacks against Check Point Security Gateways that began in late October, about a week after patches were released, exploiting the PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Attackers also used a privilege-escalation flaw in the DynamicCLI interface (CVE-2026-123039) and dropped a web shell, then a proxy, a wiper and other components. Check your gateways and web applications for web shells — that is the generic test for compromise. The federal patch deadline for CVE-2026-123039 is today, Monday, November 16.
Sources:
Source: cybersecpods.com.

item.title: Luxor bitcoin mining platform hit by AI-enabled attack
item.description:
Luxor says attackers compromised its Commander mining-management tool over the weekend and redirected customer computing power to another mining pool, in what the company called a sophisticated AI-enabled attack. Initial reports suggested about 64,000 mining machines (13 exahashes per second) were redirected to the OCEAN pool on Saturday; Luxor has not confirmed those figures and says just over a dozen customer accounts using Commander were affected. Luxor says it patched Commander within two hours of detecting the unauthorized changes and began restoring machines to their original pools, paused most feature development, and pledged full compensation to impacted customers. A Bitcoin address linked to the incident later received two OCEAN payouts totalling about 0.162 BTC, roughly $10,500.
Sources:
Source: tradersunion.com.

item.title: Russell Brand moved to HMP Littlehey; wife reads his "I am not guilty" message
item.description:
Russell Brand has been transferred from HMP Wandsworth to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a category C training and resettlement prison for men convicted of sexual offences — one of the largest such facilities in Europe. He is expected to serve two-thirds of his 10-year-and-six-month sentence before release on licence and will remain on the sex offenders register for life. His wife Laura Gallacher confirmed the move on their joint YouTube podcast on Sunday, reading out a message from Brand: "As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening." Separately, six more women have come forward with new allegations of sexual misconduct in a report by The Times and the Sunday Times, alongside Netflix's documentary "Russell Brand: Open Secret." The Metropolitan Police has passed investigations into two more rape allegations to prosecutors for a charging decision.
Sources:
Source: thenewsnow.news.
