item.title: Trump plays a waiting game as Iran raises the stakes — and the Houthis now hold the whole Bab el-Mandab Strait
item.description:
Iran fired drones at a US base in Bahrain for the second time in three days, its Houthi allies consolidated full control of the Bab el-Mandab Strait, and a tanker was attacked in the Gulf on Sunday — while President Donald Trump signalled he is in no hurry to answer, telling reporters he is handling Iran "a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly" and that "we don't need a deal with Iran." The day's events sharpened the standoff the 5 PM brief covered: Tehran is testing whether Washington will actually hit back, and so far the answer has been no.
The details filled in through the evening. Bahrain's military said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian drones on Sunday, after the Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones at a US air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base, calling it retaliation for "hostile US actions." The US Embassy in Bahrain urged Americans to exercise "heightened vigilance," citing an increased threat from Iran-backed Houthis and Iranian efforts to target US officials and facilities, and warned of possible flight cancellations and airspace closures. CNN reported that Trump has cancelled Vice President JD Vance's efforts to revive talks with Iran and told Vance to focus on domestic issues instead. The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing US officials, that Iran still holds an estimated 1,500 to 2,500 ballistic missiles despite months of American and Israeli strikes on its weapons infrastructure.
In Yemen, the picture hardened in the Houthis' favour. The New York Post reported that the Saudi-backed government forces' withdrawal leaves the Houthis in full control of the Bab el-Mandab Strait, the southern exit to the Red Sea through which about $1 trillion in goods passes each year. Houthi fighters have also nearly surrounded Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, where aid cannot get in and civilians cannot get out, and have pushed to within about 60 kilometres of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognised government. The Houthis added fresh claims on Sunday: spokesman Yahya Saree said the group fired six ballistic missiles at Saudi forces at Qa'wa camp in Lahj governorate, and that drones hit two pumping stations on the East-West oil pipeline in the Riyadh region. Saree also claimed the group shot down a Saudi armed reconnaissance aircraft over al-Jawf — unverified, with no Saudi response. The coalition said on Sunday it had intercepted two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh and three drones over the Eastern Province, and five drones across the country over Saturday and Sunday. At least 26 people have been killed in Houthi attacks on the kingdom since late September.
In the Strait of Hormuz, the day's one independently logged incident came from the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, which issued Warning 205-26: Indian shipping authorities reported an attack on a tanker sailing eastbound through the Gulf before it entered the strait, with all crew safe and the extent of damage and any environmental impact unknown. Hours later the Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers on what they called an unauthorised route in the southern strait had hit naval mines, and that one — a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude — had sunk. No vessel names, flags or owners were given, and no shipowner, flag state or naval force had confirmed a sinking by Sunday evening. US Central Command said on November 14 that more than 1.7 billion barrels of crude have moved through the strait under US military protection. The Guards' navy has declared the strait closed to any vessel that does not coordinate its passage with Tehran, while the US military says it has cleared mines from the main shipping routes.
Tehran's tone toward its neighbours also hardened. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday that the Gulf states "must be careful not to reopen old wounds," referring to their support for Iraq in the 1980s war, after the Gulf Cooperation Council suggested Iran should pay its neighbours compensation for attacks on their territory. Baghaei was asked whether Iran would accept a temporary suspension of uranium enrichment in negotiations and answered: "No. We are not at that stage at all." Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said it made no difference whether Washington wanted negotiations or war: "If the Americans make another mistake this time, the capabilities and will of Iran's armed forces will determine the geography of the battlefield." The GCC last week announced an advanced headquarters in Kuwait for its unified military command. Inside Iran, the economic squeeze is biting: long lines at gas stations, fuel shortages acknowledged by a vice president last week, and residents of Bandar Abbas blocking traffic on Thursday to protest.
Tehran's argument is that it is answering American military action, that the blockade is a direct threat to its economy and sovereignty, and that vessels sailing with tracking systems switched off on unauthorised routes are fair game. Washington's argument, as CNN framed it, is that the economic squeeze is working — Gulf oil exports are recovering, oil prices have fallen sharply from their peaks, and Iran has been unable to export any meaningful amount of its own crude for more than two months — so time is on America's side and Tehran will have to soften its terms. Riyadh and its coalition partners say the Houthi attacks are indiscriminate, aimed at airports, holy sites and civilian infrastructure, and that their interceptions are defensive. The Gulf states, for their part, have asked Trump to hold off broader strikes on Iran.
For ordinary people, the war is now a daily fact across the Gulf: Bahrain residents were woken by sirens and told to shelter, Riyadh faces regular missile alerts, Saudi airports remain disrupted, and shipping crews transit one of the world's most important oil chokepoints under threat of mines. In Yemen, about 330,000 people have been displaced by the renewed fighting, around half of them in Taiz, where aid cannot get in. Brent crude settled Friday at $95.84 a barrel; the weekend's claims had not yet been priced in when markets closed.

The day's events sharpened the standoff the 5 PM brief covered: Tehran is testing whether Washington will actually hit back, and so far the answer has been no.

item.title: Nvidia: comeback campaign grows — 160,000+ petition signatures, 7,500+ employees signed, but the sceptics are loud too
item.description:
Follow-up to the 5 PM brief's article on Jensen Huang weighing a comeback. The "Stand With Jensen" petition passed 160,000 signatures on Sunday, including more than 86,000 people identifying as shareholders and over 7,500 who identified as Nvidia employees — about 18% of the workforce. Elon Musk, Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator chief Garry Tan have signed. Deepwater's Gene Munster raised his odds of Huang returning to 51%, up from 10% on Friday. On the other side, SkyBridge founder Anthony Scaramucci said flatly "not happening," arguing this is not a sex scandal but an FBI counterintelligence review, DOJ chip-smuggling probes, a Wachtell investigation and a relationship with a direct report — "no board can reinstate a CEO it is still investigating." Analyst Dan Ives told Newsweek he sees "no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeated his call for an outsider and a "dramatic shake-up," and Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job. House China committee chair John Moolenaar said Huang and company representatives agreed to a voluntary closed-door interview, with dates still being discussed. Prediction markets are unconvinced: Kalshi traders gave Arm's Rene Haas a 24% chance of the job, Nvidia's Ian Buck 19% and Huang 13%. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday, its first since Huang's resignation.
Sources:
Source: tradingview.com.

item.title: Windows 11 now runs on the iPhone Duo — no jailbreak needed
item.description:
Google AI Studio product lead Ammaar Reshi booted the full Arm version of Windows 11 on Apple's foldable iPhone Duo without jailbreaking it, then open-sourced the project, called WindowsiOS, on GitHub on November 15. The demo shows a retail copy of Windows 11 24H2 running Microsoft Edge and Google's Antigravity coding app with touch controls. It works by translating Windows' Arm code to run on the Duo's A20 Pro chip — hardware virtualization is off the table because Apple cut hypervisor access on stock iOS starting with iOS 16.4 — and each launch needs a debugger attached. Windows gets only 4.5GB of the Duo's 12GB of RAM, and setup needs an Apple Silicon Mac running Xcode plus your own Windows 11 Arm image. Fun proof of concept, not a daily driver.
Sources:
Source: techspot.com.

item.title: CVE-2026-126173: AutomatorWP flaw lets anyone reset any WordPress admin password — no patch yet
item.description:
A critical authorization bypass (CVSS 9.8) in the AutomatorWP Pro WordPress plugin's webhook addon, versions up to and including 1.4.4, lets an unauthenticated attacker reset the password of any WordPress account — including administrators — for full account takeover. It only works when an admin has configured a specific documented automation pairing a "Receive Webhook" trigger with an "Update-User" action, but that is a supported plugin configuration. A public exploit appeared on GitHub on November 14, the day the CVE was published. No fixed version is listed yet and it is not in CISA's KEV catalog. If you run AutomatorWP, disable that webhook-to-user-update automation until a patch lands.
Sources:
Source: valtersit.com.

item.title: Catch-up: DigiCert breach exposed customer identity documents — disclosed November 5
item.description:
Certificate authority DigiCert told customers on November 5 that an internal business system archiving customer validation records had been exposed to the internet since a February 2025 migration moved it out of a VPN-restricted segment. A self-registered account without multi-factor authentication read part of the archive between June 27 and July 2, 2026; DigiCert only confirmed data access on October 19. Most of the data was business contact details, but a small minority of accounts also held identity documents submitted during certificate validation — passports, driver's licences or utility bills. No certificates were issued, changed or revoked, and DigiCert says its CA services, CertCentral and DigiCert ONE were not compromised. DigiCert has not said how many people are affected. If you submitted an ID document for a DigiCert certificate validation, treat it as exposed.
Sources:
Source: zyphe.com.

item.title: Iran fires drones at a US base in Bahrain as its allies roll back the Saudi campaign in Yemen
item.description:
Iran launched a drone attack on a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday — its second strike on the Gulf kingdom in three days — while Saudi-backed forces in Yemen pulled back from the Bab el-Mandab Strait to defend Aden, handing the Houthis their biggest gain in weeks. The two fronts moved together: Tehran is pressing the United States directly, and its allies in Yemen are pressing Saudi Arabia, with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz caught in the middle.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said six drones targeted a US air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain, calling it a "second phase" of retaliation for what it described as hostile American actions. Bahrain sounded its first nationwide threat alert since September, urging residents to stay calm and move to the nearest safe place, and said its air defences intercepted and destroyed the incoming attacks before they could reach their objectives. Explosions were heard around 4 a.m. and again around 6:30 a.m. local time, and sirens sounded across the capital, Manama. No damage or casualties have been confirmed by either Washington or Manama, and the Guards offered no evidence for their claim that the radar was hit. Two days earlier, on Friday, the Guards said they had destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain; US Central Command said it shot down two drones, with no injuries or damage. Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet.
In Yemen, the Southern Armed Forces — the main military force fighting for the internationally recognised government in the south — announced a redeployment of its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandab area, west of Taiz governorate, saying the priority was now securing the capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates. The announcement effectively ends a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea. Yemeni military sources told Reuters the forces had fallen back to al-Suqyah, about 150 km west of Aden, while Houthi fighters are now positioned just outside Tur al-Bahah, roughly 80 km from Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, which the Houthis have besieged. There was no immediate response from the Houthis or from Saudi Arabia. The Houthis had already captured the Red Sea coast and the strait in September; a Saudi-backed offensive last month retook positions around it but never fully cleared the area or retook the city of al-Mocha.
The Houthis, meanwhile, kept up their missile campaign against Saudi Arabia. On Sunday the group said it attacked King Khalid International Airport and a financial centre in Riyadh with two ballistic missiles, and two pumping stations on the East-West oil pipeline. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of those claims. The Saudi-led coalition said separately that it destroyed two Houthi drones launched toward the Mecca region and intercepted another toward Medina; Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree denied the group targets Mecca or Medina, saying its operations aim only at Saudi oil facilities and military bases. The Muslim World League condemned what it called continued Houthi attempts to target Mecca and civilian areas. Riyadh has rerouted about 4 million barrels a day of crude through the East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu — roughly 4% of global supply — as Hormuz traffic stays disrupted.
In the strait itself, the Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers were on fire on Sunday after striking naval mines, and Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported five tankers had hit mines over 48 hours, with the ISNA news agency saying one supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude had sunk. Late Sunday, Iran's army navy said separately that a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine east of the strait. None of these claims has been independently verified — no vessel names, flags or owners have been given, and maritime authorities have not confirmed any ship struck a mine. One shipping-tracking desk noted that satellite fire readings showed no heat signatures at sea across 16 passes over the strait on November 13–14. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araqchi, is due to visit Oman on Tuesday for talks; Oman holds the strait's southern shore and has acted as a mediator.
Tehran's position is that vessels using what it calls unauthorised routes with their navigation systems switched off are fair game, and that it is answering American military action against Iran. Riyadh and its coalition partners say the Houthi attacks are indiscriminate — aimed at airports, holy sites and civilian infrastructure — and that their interceptions are defensive. Washington has stayed out of direct strikes, offering intelligence and targeting help instead. Reuters reported on Saturday that Trump has said in recent days he might hold off attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Houthis, while keeping the naval blockade in place — a calculation the Bahrain strikes now test, coming weeks after the war contributed to a midterm defeat for his party.
For ordinary people, the war is now a daily fact of life across the Gulf: Bahrain residents were woken by sirens and told to shelter, Riyadh faces regular missile alerts, Saudi airports remain disrupted, and shipping crews transit one of the world's most important oil chokepoints under threat of mines. In Yemen, the human cost keeps climbing — about 300,000 people have been displaced by the latest fighting, around half of them in Taiz, where aid cannot get in and civilians cannot get out. Brent crude settled Friday at $95.84 a barrel, with futures reopening late Sunday; the weekend's claims had not yet been priced in.
In short: Iran struck directly at a US base in Bahrain for the second time in three days, its Houthi allies forced a Saudi-backed retreat from Bab el-Mandab and kept firing at Riyadh, and Tehran's latest tanker-mine claims remain unverified — while the US president's stated reason for holding off on strikes, no new provocations, is now in question.
Sources:
Source: wixx.com.

Riyadh has rerouted about 4 million barrels a day of crude through the East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu — roughly 4% of global supply — as Hormuz traffic stays disrupted.

In the strait itself, the Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers were on fire on Sunday after striking naval mines, and Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported five tankers had hit mines over 48 hours, with the ISNA news agency saying one supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude had sunk. Late Sunday, Iran's army navy said separately that a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine east of the strait. None of these claims has been independently verified — no vessel names, flags or owners have been given, and maritime authorities have not confirmed any ship struck a mine. One shipping-tracking desk noted that satellite fire readings showed no heat signatures at sea across 16 passes over the strait on November 13–14. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araqchi, is due to visit Oman on Tuesday for talks; Oman holds the strait's southern shore and has acted as a mediator.

Tehran's position is that vessels using what it calls unauthorised routes with their navigation systems switched off are fair game, and that it is answering American military action against Iran. Riyadh and its coalition partners say the Houthi attacks are indiscriminate — aimed at airports, holy sites and civilian infrastructure — and that their interceptions are defensive. Washington has stayed out of direct strikes, offering intelligence and targeting help instead. Reuters reported on Saturday that Trump has said in recent days he might hold off attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Houthis, while keeping the naval blockade in place — a calculation the Bahrain strikes now test, coming weeks after the war contributed to a midterm defeat for his party.

For ordinary people, the war is now a daily fact of life across the Gulf: Bahrain residents were woken by sirens and told to shelter, Riyadh faces regular missile alerts, Saudi airports remain disrupted, and shipping crews transit one of the world's most important oil chokepoints under threat of mines. In Yemen, the human cost keeps climbing — about 300,000 people have been displaced by the latest fighting, around half of them in Taiz, where aid cannot get in and civilians cannot get out. Brent crude settled Friday at $95.84 a barrel, with futures reopening late Sunday; the weekend's claims had not yet been priced in.

In short: Iran struck directly at a US base in Bahrain for the second time in three days, its Houthi allies forced a Saudi-backed retreat from Bab el-Mandab and kept firing at Riyadh, and Tehran's latest tanker-mine claims remain unverified — while the US president's stated reason for holding off on strikes, no new provocations, is now in question.

item.title: Ukraine hits a Su-34 test airfield and a drone base deep in Russia; Kyiv counts a week of strikes topping 2,300 drones
item.description:
Ukraine's General Staff said on Sunday that its forces struck the Akhtubinsk military airfield in Russia's Astrakhan region and a drone storage and launch facility at Tsimbulova in Oryol region, in the latest deep strikes of a campaign aimed at the infrastructure behind Russia's nightly drone waves. The two sides also kept up their exchange over Ukrainian cities, with Kyiv reporting four people killed and 69 injured across the country over the past day.
The Akhtubinsk airfield houses the 929th State Flight Test Centre and is a primary base for Su-34 fighter-bombers that launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities; the General Staff said the strike triggered secondary explosions at an ammunition depot storing guided aerial missile components and hit a mobile radar altimeter. The governor of Astrakhan region said 31 drones were shot down in the northern part of the region overnight. The second target, the Tsimbulova drone base, is a facility from which Russian forces launch attack drones toward Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure. The strikes follow Saturday night's hits on the Nizhnekamskneftekhim petrochemical complex and a refinery in Tatarstan and a defence plant in Bryansk, which were covered in this morning's brief. As with those, the extent of the damage could not be independently verified.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that over the past week alone, Russian forces launched more than 2,300 attack drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles of various types at Ukraine, and that on Sunday the national grid operator, Ukrenergo, imposed emergency disconnections in parts of Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk after strikes damaged electrical equipment. Russian officials reported two fatalities after Ukrainian drones damaged electrical substations in Taganrog, in the Rostov region. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 132 long-range drones overnight Saturday into Sunday, 106 of them intercepted, with hits at 20 locations — figures reported in the morning brief.
Zelensky also said a 161 km/h speed cap on Starshield satellite terminals operating over Russian-occupied territory has now persisted for five consecutive days, and that it is letting more Russian drones through because Ukraine's frontline interceptor drones cannot catch the fast, jet-powered Shaheds, which travel at 450–500 km/h. Kyiv says it will raise the issue with partners ahead of Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara's Brussels visit and the Ramstein contact group meeting on Tuesday, November 17. Khmara also announced that Canada is funding PAC-3 Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine through the JUMPSTART mechanism.
Kyiv's argument is that Russia is systematically dismantling the power supply ordinary Ukrainians depend on as temperatures drop, and that the US is undercutting Ukraine's defences at the same time. Moscow frames its strikes as aimed at military and logistics targets — railways, ports and substations feeding the war effort — and says its air defences are swatting down Ukrainian drones in large numbers. SpaceX has not publicly explained the Starshield limits, and Washington has said nothing new about the dispute.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the practical effect is the same as it has been all autumn: power cuts, damaged homes and disrupted trains, with emergency blackouts now a regular feature of the week. Ukraine's deep strikes into Tatarstan, Astrakhan and Oryol are meant to raise the cost for Moscow and hit the bases launching the attacks, but they have not stopped the nightly drone waves.
In short: Ukraine hit a Su-34 test airfield and a drone launch base deep inside Russia, Russia kept hammering Ukraine's power grid with a week of attacks topping 2,300 drones, and Kyiv is heading into Tuesday's Ramstein meeting pressing allies over the Starshield speed cap and air-defence supplies.
Sources:
Source: kimkj.com.

item.title: Nvidia: Huang is weighing a comeback as allies organize a "war room" to lobby the board
item.description:
Jensen Huang is considering a return as Nvidia's chief executive, days after he resigned over reports of extramarital affairs — including one with a woman described in reports as a suspected Chinese spy — the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. The report marks a new phase in the leadership crisis at the world's most valuable chipmaker, with the ousted founder's allies now organizing openly to get him back.
According to the FT, Huang has discussed the possibility of returning with confidants, and one ally said they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return and would try to garner support from the White House. "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the ally said, adding that the efforts had Huang's support. Elon Musk and Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney have already backed a public letter calling for Huang's reinstatement, and a petition urging the board to bring him back passed 135,000 signatures over the weekend. Two large shareholders, Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management, wrote to the board on Friday urging a slow, measured search and asking it to keep Huang's potential return on the table — without calling for immediate reinstatement.
The pushback is real, though. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a broader leadership shake-up at the company, according to reports, and the board has already approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a possible successor, the FT reported on Friday. Nvidia has not yet hired a search firm, and interim chief executive Colette Kress — the company's chief financial officer — leads her first earnings call on Tuesday, November 17, with a company-wide meeting scheduled for Wednesday. Huang has accepted a closed-door congressional appearance before Thanksgiving and is scheduled to testify under oath before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3; House Republicans have separately asked him to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10. The board's independent investigation, run by the law firm Wachtell Lipton, continues, and the Justice Department has not concluded whether Alice Huang — the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the affair reports — was a spy, a claim Beijing denies.
Huang's supporters argue he built Nvidia into the engine of the AI industry, that he deserves due process while the investigation establishes the facts, and that removing him mid-crisis risks the company. The board's defenders — and the critics pushing for a clean break — argue the questions go beyond the affairs themselves: Reuters reported Huang misled Nvidia's general counsel and chief marketing officer about the nature of his dealings with Alice Huang, describing them as standard business, and the reports raise unresolved questions about exports of advanced AI chips to China. Nvidia's stock has fallen more than 30% from its October 6 closing high, wiping out more than $1.8 trillion in market value.
For ordinary investors and the wider tech industry, the stakes are immediate: Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, its first since Huang's resignation, and the company's leadership — and with it, the direction of the AI chip business that underpins much of the industry — is now openly contested between the board, the founder's allies, and Washington.
In short: Huang is weighing a comeback and his allies are organizing to lobby the board and the White House, the board is still searching for a successor and has approached Arm's chief executive, and Tuesday's earnings will be the first public test of the company without him.
Sources:
Source: wncy.com.

item.title: Apple: Gurman says Face ID on the iPhone Duo 2 is a toss-up — report, not confirmed
item.description:
Bloomberg's Mark Gurman said in his Sunday Power On newsletter that Apple has built iPhone Duo 2 prototypes with Face ID on the outer display, but engineers are still working to integrate it and the company is running out of time to lock in the hardware for a fall 2027 launch — so the feature may slip to the Duo 3. Gurman's four goals for future Duo models: Face ID, an Action button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter design. Apple has said nothing about the plans, and customer feedback on the current Duo won't change the hardware until the third generation. This is a roadmap report, not an announcement.
Sources:
Source: macrumors.com.

item.title: Google: Gemini's Wallet link can now read bank accounts too — opt-in, read-only
item.description:
Follow-up to this morning's brief: Google's Gemini-to-Wallet connection, which rolled out in the US on Friday, November 13, also lets users optionally link bank, credit card, loan and investment accounts through the fintech firm Plaid. Gemini can read the numbers to answer questions about spending, budgets, cash flow and subscriptions, but cannot move money, pay a bill or buy anything. The feature is opt-in, off by default, English-only at launch, and limited to users 18 and older with a personal Google account.

item.title: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday: ~1,093 fixes, one exploited Outlook zero-day that leaks login hashes — catch-up
item.description:
Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday, released Tuesday, November 10, fixed roughly 1,093 vulnerabilities, 63 of them rated Critical — the second straight month over 1,000. The one that matters most is an actively exploited Outlook zero-day, CVE-2026-124194 (CVSS 6.5, rated Moderate): opening a specially crafted message file makes Outlook connect to an attacker-controlled server without the usual external-content warning, leaking the user's NTLMv2 hash, which an attacker can crack or relay to impersonate the user. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector — the file has to be opened — but CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, with a federal remediation deadline of November 24. The fix ships in the Office/Microsoft 365 updates, not the Windows cumulative update, so a Windows patch alone does not close it. A second flaw, CVE-2026-123158 in Mariner, is also in KEV. Counts vary by source (1,093 per Ivanti and Splashtop; up to 1,259 by another tally), but the exploited Outlook flaw is the same in every count.
Sources:
Source: sandpczone.com.

item.title: Russell Brand: wife speaks out from prison message; six more women have come forward
item.description:
Russell Brand, sentenced on November 9 to ten years and six months for rape and three sexual assaults, sent a message from prison on Sunday through his wife, Laura Gallacher, who spoke about the conviction on the couple's weekly YouTube series, "Sunday Service with the Brands." Brand, 51, says he is innocent and is being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire — a low-security prison holding around 1,200 male sexual offenders — after being transferred there on Friday from HMP Wandsworth. He must serve two-thirds of his sentence before parole and will remain on the sex offenders register for life. Separately, six additional women have accused Brand of sexual misconduct in incidents between 2005 and 2015 that could not be included in the recent trial, and police are reviewing reports from roughly six to eight more women, which could lead to further charges. One accuser, Mia Latter, has waived her anonymity and alleges Brand orally raped her in 2006 when she was 16. The government's independent adviser on sexual offences, Professor Katrin Hohl, said on Sunday that the public attention around the trial should prompt a proper examination of how people who report sexual offences are treated in court, including the use of false ideas about sexual assault and the directions judges give juries.
Sources:
Source: pagesix.com.

item.title: Likud and Yashar teams met today; no outcome reported yet
item.description:
The Likud and Yashar negotiating teams met on Sunday as scheduled — a meeting fixed before Netanyahu's public appeal on Saturday for unity talks "without preconditions," which Eisenkot dismissed as "spin" and "tricks." No outcome from the meeting had been reported by Sunday evening. The Knesset speaker vote is Tuesday, November 17 at 4 p.m., with Matan Kahana (Yashar) nominated to replace Netanyahu ally Amir Ohana — the first real test of whether Eisenkot has the numbers. The Change bloc also plans to advance bills on Wednesday repealing legislation affecting the attorney general's authority and the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee. Eisenkot's mandate runs to December 6, with a possible 14-day extension.
Sources:
Source: srnnews.com.

item.title: Russia pounds Ukraine's power grid and railways overnight; Ukraine hits back deep inside Russia
item.description:
Russia launched one of its heaviest drone nights of the month against Ukraine overnight from Saturday into Sunday, hitting energy and railway infrastructure in eight regions, while Ukraine struck a major petrochemical plant and an oil refinery deep inside Russia. The exchange comes as winter closes in and with no ceasefire of any kind in effect.
Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 132 long-range attack drones, 78 of them jet-powered, starting Saturday evening, and that 106 were shot down or suppressed by Sunday morning, with hits recorded at 20 locations. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks mainly targeted power substations, struck with Shahed-type drones, and hit infrastructure in Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv and five other regions. In the Odesa region, a DTEK energy facility was hit and about 41,000 homes lost power, with the operator warning repairs will take time. Russian missiles also struck near Vyshhorod outside Kyiv, and jet-powered drones set fire to an industrial facility near Kropyvnytskyi. Guided aerial bombs damaged apartment blocks in Zaporizhzhia, injuring six people including a two-year-old. Russia's defence ministry, for its part, confirmed strikes on substations, port infrastructure and locomotives, and said a bulk carrier heading for Odesa was hit — claims that could not be independently verified.
Ukraine answered overnight with strikes of its own. Its General Staff said Ukrainian forces hit the Nizhnekamskneftekhim petrochemical plant — a major producer of rubber and plastics — and an oil refining facility in Russia's Tatarstan region, more than 1,000 km from the front, as well as the Monolit defence and aviation plant in Bryansk region, which makes helicopters and spare parts. Neither side's claims about the extent of the damage could be independently verified, and the two militaries released sharply conflicting tallies, with Moscow claiming to have downed hundreds of Ukrainian drones.
Zelensky again pointed the finger at SpaceX's Starshield service, saying many Russian strikes are getting through because speed restrictions on Starshield terminals along the front line and in occupied territory are still in place. "The Russians are targeting substations with 'shaheds'. And many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there," he said. Kyiv has raised the Starshield issue repeatedly since October, when Ukrainian officials said restrictions disrupted military operations during a ballistic missile barrage; SpaceX has not publicly explained the limits.
Kyiv's argument is that Russia is systematically dismantling the power supply ordinary Ukrainians depend on as temperatures drop, and that the US is undercutting Ukraine's defences at the same time. Moscow frames its strikes as aimed at military and logistics targets — railways, ports and substations feeding the war effort — and says its air defences are swatting down Ukrainian drones in large numbers. Washington, meanwhile, has said nothing new about the Starshield dispute, and Trump has accused Zelensky of "not wanting" to end the war, a charge Kyiv rejects.
For ordinary people, the practical effect is the same as it has been all autumn: power cuts, damaged homes and disrupted trains. Around 41,000 households in the Odesa region woke up without electricity on Sunday, repairs are expected to take time, and the Zaporizhzhia apartment strike is a reminder that the campaign is hitting residential areas as well as infrastructure. Ukraine's deep strikes into Tatarstan are meant to raise the cost for Moscow, but they have not stopped the nightly drone waves.
In short: the nightly war of attrition on infrastructure is grinding on with no pause in sight — Russia hit power and rail in eight regions, Ukraine hit a petrochemical plant and refinery far behind Russian lines, and the Starshield dispute between Kyiv and Washington is still unresolved.
Sources:
Source: img.statement.com.

item.title: Three tankers ablaze in Hormuz as Iran confirms a mine strike; Riyadh intercepts more Houthi missiles
item.description:
Iran's navy has confirmed that a mine strike in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday set three oil tankers ablaze, and Saudi air defences intercepted two more Houthi ballistic missiles over Riyadh on Sunday, as the Gulf conflict keeps tightening its grip on shipping, markets and daily life across the region.
The Iranian navy confirmation, reported by state media and carried by Reuters on Sunday, is a notable shift: for weeks Tehran has claimed tanker mine strikes that maritime authorities could not verify, and it gave no vessel names, flags or owners this time either. Separately, the Saudi-led coalition said on Sunday it had downed two ballistic missiles fired at Riyadh along with three drones over the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province. The UK's maritime trade body, UKMTO, also issued a fresh warning (205-26) about an attack on a tanker transiting the Gulf eastbound before it entered the strait, based on an Indian shipping report; the crew are safe and the vessel, the means of attack and the attacker are not named. Gulf stock markets slid on Sunday on the news — Saudi Arabia's benchmark down 0.7%, Qatar down 1.8%.
Inside Yemen, the ground war shifted as well. Yemeni government forces withdrew from Dhubab airport and the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and Houthi media claimed control of the Lahj coast — a claim no independent party has verified. Local sources reported that a missile hit cars carrying displaced people in Khor Omaira, Lahj, killing 8 civilians and wounding 14, though there is no official confirmation and it is unclear who fired it. Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, seaports and energy installations have intensified in recent days, and Riyadh has answered by expanding its air campaign against Houthi targets in Yemen.
Tehran's position, as stated by its navy and foreign ministry, is that vessels using what it calls unauthorised routes with their navigation systems switched off are fair game, and that it will not leave attacks unanswered. Riyadh and its coalition partners say the Houthi attacks are indiscriminate — aimed at airports, holy sites and civilian infrastructure — and that their interceptions are defensive. Washington has stayed out of direct strikes, offering intelligence and targeting help instead, and US officials have said they expect no US airstrikes before the November 3 midterms. The wider region is hedging: Turkey and Qatar sealed a mutual defence pact on Friday, pledging a united front against any foreign armed attack on either country, and a long-standing Qatari LNG contract has been cancelled on force majeure grounds — the first since the conflict began — with analysts saying Poland's Orlen could save up to $2 billion from the cancellation.
For ordinary people in the region, the war is now a daily fact of life: Riyadh residents face regular missile alerts, Saudi airports remain disrupted, shipping crews transit one of the world's most important oil chokepoints under threat of mines, and Gulf markets are sliding. The displaced families killed at Khor Omaira are a reminder that the heaviest price is still being paid by Yemeni civilians caught between the two sides.
In short: Iran has now confirmed a mine strike that set three tankers ablaze, the Houthis keep firing at Riyadh, the coalition keeps intercepting, and the ground war in Yemen is moving in the Houthis' favour at Bab el-Mandab — with no sign of de-escalation from any side.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Trump–Putin–Xi trilateral confirmed for Thursday in Shenzhen — but Ukraine is off the agenda
item.description:
The Kremlin confirmed on Saturday that Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump will meet on Thursday, November 19, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen — the first-ever trilateral meeting of the three leaders. The White House announced the meeting on Friday; Beijing has still not confirmed it will take place. A senior US official said the agenda is nuclear arms control and Iran, and that Ukraine is not on it — Washington says the Ukraine war is handled on a separate US–Russia track. No agreement is expected; officials describe it as a first conversation on nuclear reductions since the last US–Russia treaty, New START, expired in February. Zelensky has objected to Ukraine's future being discussed without Kyiv at the table, and European leaders in Dublin reiterated that European security cannot be decided without Europe. No separate Trump–Putin one-on-one is scheduled.
Sources:
Source: tbsnews.net.

item.title: Nvidia: "Stand with Jensen" petition passes 135,000; Huang to testify to Senate Banking Committee on December 3

Separately, Huang has accepted a closed-door congressional appearance before Thanksgiving and is scheduled to testify under oath before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3. item.title: Microsoft 365 outage and FAA ground stop both resolved — and both blamed on routine upgrades, not attacks
item.description:
Microsoft says its Microsoft 365 outage is over. The disruption ran about 36 hours from Thursday into Friday, cutting off Outlook, Teams and Copilot for users in more than 70 countries; Microsoft says it was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, exposing a latent bug. The company says there was no cyber activity involved and promised a preliminary report within two business days. Separately, the FAA's nationwide ground stop on Friday — about four and a half hours, with roughly 7,000–10,000 flights delayed or cancelled — was caused by a router flooding the air traffic control network during a contractor's copper-to-fiber telecom cutover at a remote site. Officials say it was not a cyberattack, and the FAA administrator said schedules should be back to normal by late Sunday. Both incidents were still unfolding in Saturday's briefs; the causes are now confirmed as technical failures, though neither formal report has been published yet.
Sources:
Source: geekwire.com.

item.title: Likud and Yashar negotiating teams meet today; committee chairs being carved up
item.description:
The Likud and Yashar negotiating teams meet today (Sunday) to discuss a possible unity government, a meeting fixed before Netanyahu's public appeal on Saturday — which Eisenkot dismissed as "spin" and "tricks." The teams: Yashar sends Yoav Horowitz and Chili Tropper; Likud sends Ofir Katz and Michael Rabello. Meanwhile the Eisenkot bloc is consolidating control of key Knesset committees: Yair Golan's Democratic Party will chair the special committee reviewing Netanyahu's judicial reform, and Avigdor Liberman is set to chair Foreign Affairs and Defense. The Knesset speaker vote is Tuesday, November 17 at 4 PM, with Matan Kahana (Yashar) nominated — the first real test of whether Eisenkot has the numbers. Eisenkot's mandate runs to December 6, with a possible 14-day extension.
Sources:
Source: democrata.es.

item.title: "Bring him back": 115,000 sign a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's board weighs a slow search — and Asia scrambles to lock in chip supply
item.description:
The fight over Nvidia's empty chief executive chair turned public on Saturday, with more than 115,000 people — including nearly 6,000 current Nvidia employees and Elon Musk — signing a petition demanding Jensen Huang's reinstatement, while two big shareholders asked the board to slow down and keep Huang's return on the table. Governments across Asia, meanwhile, moved to confirm their chip supply, and questions grew over whether Nvidia will stay the open-source AI champion Huang built it into.
The "Stand with Jensen" petition had attracted more than 115,000 signatures by Saturday afternoon, according to TechCrunch. Its website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders — though those affiliations are self-reported and the campaign says its screening does not verify identities. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk, Replit chief Amjad Masad, Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator chief Garry Tan. The petition says its signers are "concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process" and demands the board "bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts." Its slogan: "Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice."
Separately, Altimeter Capital chief Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker posted a letter on X on Friday asking the board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia" — and to keep "the potential return of Jensen Huang" on the table. CNBC reported on the letter on Saturday, and was careful to note what it did not say: it did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement. Nvidia was Altimeter's largest disclosed equity holding, a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30, and the two firms together disclosed about $2.13 billion of Nvidia stock. The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim chief Colette Kress in the meantime.
Huang resigned on Thursday, four days after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, a chip executive US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy. The board's independent investigation, launched November 8, is still running. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, and news reports have suggested he engaged in multiple extramarital affairs. On Friday, the Financial Times reported the board had approached Arm chief Rene Haas as a possible successor, with no guarantee of an offer. Kress, the chief financial officer, is interim chief executive while the board searches, and Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, November 17 — her first call in the job. The stock is down more than 30 percent since its early-October high, erasing over $1.8 trillion in value.
The fallout is already reaching governments that depend on Nvidia's chips. China's foreign ministry rejected the spy allegations on November 10 as groundless and a smear against Beijing, and on Friday said it was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Reuters reported more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia's restricted processors now face uncertainty. In Singapore, authorities seized Alice Huang's passport in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations about server purchases; in February 2026 police found insufficient evidence to establish offenses, but said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed — she was warned and barred from re-entering Singapore, and the investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. South Korea's Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and continue joint AI projects, after the government's AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday. Taiwan's economy minister said Huang's departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, and Taipei said Nvidia's planned overseas headquarters there remained on track. Japan's Industry Ministry said it would closely monitor Nvidia, calling the company an important player in Japan's AI semiconductor industry.
The two camps are arguing past each other. The petitioners and the two investors frame this as a due-process question: a founder-CEO removed in days, before an investigation has established the facts, and a board that should not rush to close the door on him. The board, for its part, has said nothing about the petition, has not formally engaged any successor candidate, and is running what it describes as a deliberate search — while Kress runs the company. Beijing flatly denies the espionage allegation at the center of the scandal; US officials, including a classified memo from Secretary of State Rubio this spring, have said Chinese intelligence recruited Alice Huang. Neither side's claim about her has been proven in public.
The uncertainty now extends to Nvidia's $12.3 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, the open-source AI hub, agreed in September and facing Justice Department antitrust scrutiny ahead of a planned close in the first half of 2027. Huang was the tech industry's most prominent corporate champion of open-weight AI models — he wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies earlier this year urging Washington not to over-restrict them — and his exit leaves that commitment in doubt. Hugging Face chief Clement Delangue posted on X that the platform will keep advocating for open-source AI regardless of the leadership change, and a company insider told TechCrunch that development of Nvidia's own open-weight Nemotron models is not expected to be disrupted. But industry observers question whether a future chief executive will put the same capital and personal intensity behind open weights.
For ordinary people, the stakes are less about one executive and more about the hardware the whole AI boom runs on: governments from Seoul to Tokyo are already checking their chip supply, more than $3 billion of Chinese AI projects are in limbo, and the open models millions of developers build on — hosted on Hugging Face — now depend on a company whose next leader has not yet been chosen. If the board picks a chief who pulls back from open weights, the open-source AI ecosystem loses its biggest corporate backer just as Washington debates restricting it.
In short: a 115,000-signature petition and two major shareholders are pushing Nvidia's board to keep Jensen Huang's return possible, while Asian governments scramble to secure chip supply and the fate of the $12.3 billion Hugging Face deal hangs on whoever runs Nvidia next. Watch Tuesday's earnings — Kress's first call as interim chief — for the first real signal of where the company goes from here.
Sources:
Source: techcrunch.com.

item.title: Russia asks for a local ceasefire in Kostyantynivka — Kyiv suspects a trap
item.description:
The Kremlin has asked for a temporary localized ceasefire in Kostyantynivka, and President Zelensky responded on Saturday, according to the Institute for the Study of War's November 14 assessment. ISW assesses the proposed pause would likely let Russia reinforce the southern flank of its "Fortress Belt" and set conditions for renewed efforts to seize Kostyantynivka and Dobropillya. A Ukrainian military source reported on November 13 that Russian forces began deploying heavy equipment toward Dobropillya itself, and the commander of Ukraine's 1st Azov Corps, Brigadier General Denys Prokopenko, has warned since mid-September that Russia was preparing mechanized assaults in that direction. Russian forces are using autumn fog, wind and rain — which degrade Ukrainian reconnaissance and strike drones — to advance. Why it matters: the ceasefire request mirrors the one in occupied Oleshky in late October, and Kyiv is treating it as a battlefield maneuver, not a humanitarian gesture.
Sources:
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: Russia is hitting Kyiv's bridges and has destroyed 400 locomotives this year
item.description:
Russian forces have intensified strikes against Kyiv's Northern, Southern and Paton bridges since September, according to a Kremlin-affiliated military blogger cited by ISW — part of an effort to break the city's power grid into two halves across the Dnipro River. Separately, Ukraine's infrastructure minister told parliament on November 13 that Russia has destroyed 630 Ukrainian locomotives since the full-scale invasion began, including 400 in 2026 alone — 63 percent of all rolling stock destroyed in the war. Russian forces also introduced a ground-launched variant of the Dan-T loitering munition this week. Why it matters: the bridge campaign targets the power grid's geography, and the locomotive losses are strangling the rail logistics Ukraine's war economy runs on.
Sources:
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: Saudi foreign minister heads to Brussels; G7 condemned Iran and the Houthis
item.description:
Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan arrived in Brussels on Saturday, November 14, to attend the European Union Foreign Affairs Council meeting on Monday, November 16, according to the Saudi Press Agency. The EU foreign ministers are expected to discuss freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab, and Germany's foreign office said the ministers had already condemned a Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport. Separately, the G7 foreign ministers' joint declaration from their November 9–10 meeting in Paris — the group's strongest language on Gulf security since the crisis intensified — "strongly condemned Iran's attacks against its neighbours" and "the obstruction of transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz," and condemned "in the strongest terms" the Houthis' continued strikes on Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has been pushing the EU to designate the Houthis as a terrorist organization. Why it matters: the diplomacy is shifting from statements to institutional steps — an EU terror designation would be the first of its kind for the Houthis from a major bloc.
Sources:
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Iran's tanker-mine claims: five in two days, still unverified
item.description:
Iran's naval forces claimed five commercial vessels struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz across November 13–14 — three on Friday and two more on Saturday, including a liquefied gas carrier and a very large crude carrier. No maritime authority has confirmed any of them, no vessel names or flags have been given, and ISW says it has seen no indicators Iran has successfully re-mined the southern route, which US Central Command said it fully demined on August 27. The claims now stress that the vessels were under US escort, which ISW reads as an information operation to undermine confidence in US escort operations. Why it matters: the claims are the story either way — if believed, they push shipping toward Iranian-controlled waters; if not, they are a pressure campaign with no confirmed sinkings behind it.
Sources:
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: Apple is changing how it builds iOS and macOS, Gurman reports
item.description:
Apple has changed its development process for iOS 28, macOS 28 and corresponding software updates, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, cited in MacRumors' Saturday roundup — giving engineers more time to explore and develop new features within the existing update cycles. The same roundup notes Apple says more than 100,000 apps have now been optimized for the iPhone Duo's foldable form factor, and that Apple released iOS 27.2.1 this week with security-related fixes. Why it matters: a slower, more deliberate software cycle is a notable shift for a company that ships a major iOS version every September — and the iPhone Duo app count is the first real measure of whether developers are embracing the foldable.
Sources:
Source: macrumors.com.

item.title: Fullerton Health breach exposed about 140,000 migrant worker records in Singapore
item.description:
Fullerton Health and Singapore's Ministry of Manpower said on November 14 that about 140,000 work pass holder records were compromised through a standalone server behind the Migrant Worker Primary Care Plan portal — about 43,000 of them for passes that are no longer valid. Singapore's Cyber Security Agency said at least 12 incidents hit Singapore organizations or their providers between October 24 and November 13, six of them in healthcare and community care, with monthly reports since September running at three times the January–August average. Why it matters: it is the largest of a run of Singapore healthcare breaches, and the third in the sector in a month.
Sources:
Source: cvetodo.com.

item.title: Four open-source projects got CVEs in two days — none exploited yet
item.description:
Four unrelated open-source projects received CVEs on November 13–14, and fixes are already out for all of them: JSON::XS 4.05 fixes seven parser vulnerabilities, including a one-byte heap write in the incremental parser; goose (the AI coding agent) had a command-execution flaw in goose review (CVE-2026-129128, CVSS 8.4) where a malicious .git/config could run commands as the user — fixed in 1.53.0, and the maintainers deleted the command from main on November 12; C-Kermit 11.1.515 fixes eleven CVEs including server-side remote code execution (CVSS 9.2); and Seafile's SeaDoc converter had a flaw (CVE-2026-129167, CVSS 9.2) where any token signed with the shared JWT key — including the read-only token embedded in public share pages — was accepted. No exploitation has been reported for any of the four. Why it matters: the goose and SeaDoc bugs are the dangerous kind — they take attacker input by design, so patching is not optional.
Sources:
Source: corgea.com.

item.title: FBI: some ARTEX intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours
item.description:
The FBI says some intrusions using ARTEX — the open-source AI autonomous penetration-testing tool released in October — went from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours, according to the November 14 threat report. Cisco Talos also found more than 700 reachable PentAGI instances exposed on the internet. ARTEX was covered in the October 12 brief; this is the first FBI comment on how fast it is being used in the wild. Why it matters: offensive AI tooling is compressing the time defenders have to detect and respond from days to hours.
Sources:
Source: cvetodo.com.

item.title: React2Shell is still being exploited — one server hit on Saturday
item.description:
React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182), the remote code execution bug in React Server Components fixed in Next.js 15.2.6 almost a year ago, is still being actively exploited in November 2026. One company documented its own server being hit on November 14: the attacker got in through the public Next.js bug between November 8–14, and on Saturday dropped an XMRig Monero miner. The hosting provider stopped the server 23 minutes later, and the company rebuilt from scratch in under five hours. Single-source account, but it matches the wider pattern of unpatched Next.js servers still being mined. Why it matters: a patch that is almost a year old is still not applied everywhere, and the attackers know it.
Sources:
Source: zettabyteincorp.com.

item.title: CISA KEV: no new additions; Monday deadlines loom
item.description:
No new flaws were added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Saturday. The two additions from Friday — Check Point CVE-2026-123039 and UnrealIRCd CVE-2026-114713 — carry a federal patch deadline of Monday, November 16. The Check Point attack chain (PHP2Shell flaws CVE-2026-109618/109619, both CVSS 9.2, chained to the privilege-escalation flaw) hit a couple of dozen customers in two waves, late October and November 2, with a wiper run against VMware ESXi hosts in the Israel-focused first wave.
Sources:

item.title: Israel coalition: the quotes behind Saturday's standoff
item.description:
No new moves in Israel's coalition talks on Saturday evening beyond the exchange already covered in the 5 PM brief — but the exact wording is now out. Netanyahu, in a video statement, said Iran "will not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us" and argued a narrow government could not meet the threat. Eisenkot replied about an hour later: "Nice try, but these tricks don't work on me," calling the appeal "another spin" and noting Likud–Yashar negotiating teams were already due to meet Sunday, November 15. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich backed Netanyahu on X: "Gadi, the time has come." The Knesset speaker vote is set for Tuesday, November 17 at 4 p.m., with Eisenkot's nominee Matan Kahana as the test of Likud's good faith. Eisenkot holds the mandate until December 6, with a possible 14-day extension from President Herzog. Why it matters: the speaker vote on Tuesday is the first real test of whether either side's unity talk is serious.
Sources:
Source: silentdossier.com.

item.title: Ukraine hits Russia's biggest oil-blending hub and a bomber airbase — as Moscow rules out any land swap
item.description:
Ukraine struck two high-value targets deep inside Russia on Friday, its General Staff announced on Saturday: the Samara oil transfer station — the hub where Russia blends its flagship Urals export crude — and the Lipetsk-2 military airfield, home to the Su-34 bombers that drop glide bombs on Ukrainian cities. The same day, Moscow's chief negotiator flatly ruled out the territorial trade at the heart of this week's diplomacy, saying there is "no possibility" of exchanging land.
According to Ukraine's General Staff, long-range drones hit the Samara linear production and dispatch station near the village of Prosvet, about 950 kilometers east of Ukrainian-controlled territory, setting several crude oil storage tanks ablaze. Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said its Alpha special operations center carried out the strike and confirmed hits on storage tanks. The station is one of the most important nodes in Russia's energy export system: it receives crude by pipeline from Tatarstan, western Siberia and Kazakhstan and blends it into Urals, which accounts for up to half of Russia's crude oil exports. It covers more than 216 hectares and holds 71 storage tanks with a combined capacity above 1.6 million cubic meters. Samara's regional governor, Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, confirmed a drone attack on an industrial site in the region and said four people were killed, though he did not say what was hit. The facility has been struck repeatedly — this was the sixth attack since October 2, and Ukrainian outlets report roughly 40 percent of its tank system was already damaged or destroyed by October 11. A separate analysis notes that in the last 15 days Ukraine has hit 13 refineries and oil-and-gas facilities, including all six of Russia's largest refineries.
The second strike hit Lipetsk-2 airfield, more than 340 kilometers east of the Ukrainian border. According to the General Staff, a hangar storing specialized aircraft maintenance equipment, aviation fuel tanks and the airfield's central command-and-control post were hit on November 13. The base hosts Su-34, Su-35 and MiG-31 aircraft, and Lipetsk-2 has been targeted repeatedly before — Ukrainian military intelligence says pro-Ukrainian partisans set fire to two Su-30 jets at a Lipetsk-area airfield in December 2025. There is no independent picture of the damage at either site, and Moscow has not issued a response on the strikes themselves.
The two sides are now publicly talking past each other on the diplomacy. On Wednesday, after two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky told state news agency TASS there is "no possibility" of a territorial exchange between Russia and Ukraine, adding that "every inch of Russian land will be recovered, one way or another" and that Russia's buffer zone along the border would keep expanding. That directly answers the idea President Zelensky revealed this morning — that US negotiators in Abu Dhabi had floated Ukraine withdrawing from Donbas in exchange for NATO membership. Zelensky said Ukraine will not give up territory; Medinsky says Russia will not give any back. The Abu Dhabi talks did produce one thing both sides reported: an agreement in principle on a major prisoner exchange. US mediators said the talks showed a lack of trust between the warring sides, with territory the central unresolved issue.
For ordinary people, the Samara strike is the war's economic front made visible: Urals crude pays for Russia's war effort, and Ukraine's campaign against refineries and blending hubs is aimed at the money, not just the battlefield. Russian regions have already begun reintroducing fuel rationing as processing capacity falls, and the International Energy Agency said Russian oil processing will be "severely curtailed" through year-end. On the Ukrainian side, the overnight toll reported this morning — seven killed and 80 injured across the country, including a family killed in Belgorod and 50,000 without power in Odesa — is a reminder that the strikes go both ways and civilians pay for both.
In short: Ukraine hit the heart of Russia's oil-export system and a bomber base in one day, while Moscow ruled out any territorial swap — closing the door on the Donbas-for-NATO idea Zelensky says Washington floated. Watch whether the prisoner-exchange agreement holds, and whether the November 19 trilateral in Shenzhen produces anything beyond the nuclear-arms and Iran agenda it is officially about.
Sources:
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Gulf escalation goes to the UN as the US warns Americans in Saudi Arabia — and the fighting shifts to Yemen's south
item.description:
The Gulf standoff moved into the UN Security Council on Friday, the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a nationwide warning to Americans the same day, and the Houthis opened a new front against Yemeni government forces in the south — a day in which every side told a different story about the same war.
The Security Council met on Friday at Bahrain's request to discuss threats to maritime security in the Persian Gulf. The Gulf Cooperation Council's secretary-general told the Council that since February 28, GCC states have faced Iranian strikes involving more than 7,000 missiles and drones targeting airports, ports, oil and gas facilities, power stations, desalination plants and residential areas, and that roughly 1,600 vessels have been disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz with more than 23,000 seafarers stranded. A UN official cited International Maritime Organization data: 134 incidents and 25 seafarer deaths in the strait and the wider Middle East maritime area as of November 11, with October the worst month for shipping attacks since February. Lloyd's List put the October figure at 37 ship attacks in the Hormuz area — the highest monthly total since the war began — with at least 14 confirmed so far in November. Iran's ambassador blamed the instability on US and Israeli military action; the Gulf states accused Iran and the Houthis.
Hours earlier, the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a nationwide security alert on November 13 warning American citizens of an increased Houthi attack threat, urging "extreme caution" at the kingdom's airports and telling Americans to stay away from sites linked to Western interests. It landed the same day the Houthis claimed drone strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and the East-West oil pipeline, and as the Revolutionary Guard claimed more tanker mine strikes in the strait — claims no maritime authority has confirmed.
On the ground in Yemen, the Institute for the Study of War reports the Houthis launched ballistic missile salvos on November 13 and 14 at Yemeni government-aligned forces' staging areas and weapons depots in Lahij and Aden governorates — Jabal Kharaz and Khor Amira in Madaribah wa al Arah district, and Aden city — aiming to disrupt the logistics behind a government offensive in southeastern Lahij. Government-aligned forces have nonetheless kept recapturing territory, consolidating control of the Sarih junction, and Saudi aircraft have provided close air support, striking Houthi commanders, fighters and vehicles on the frontline and hitting reinforcements moving south from al Turbah. The Houthis also claimed strikes on Saudi targets on November 13 — drones at King Khalid International Airport and an East-West Pipeline pumping station, and ballistic missiles at Saudi forces in Tuwaal, Jazan province. Saudi Arabia separately intercepted Houthi drones near Riyadh and southern Saudi Arabia on November 14, according to the coalition. The Houthi-run Health Ministry said 12 civilians were killed in a Saudi airstrike on a market in Taiz on Saturday — a claim with no independent confirmation.
Meanwhile Iran's mine claims keep coming with no verification. The Revolutionary Guard Navy claimed on November 13 that a liquefied gas carrier and two oil tankers struck mines and exploded or caught fire on "unauthorized routes," and the regular navy claimed another tanker hit a mine east of the strait on November 14. ISW notes Iran has recently started emphasizing in its claims that the vessels were under US escort, in what looks like an information operation to discredit US escort operations — and that it has seen no indicators Iran has successfully re-mined the southern route, which US Central Command said it fully demined on August 27.
For ordinary people, the practical picture is unchanged but hardening: shipping through the strait is still running roughly 65 percent below pre-war volume, the US Embassy is telling Americans to avoid Saudi airports and Western-linked sites, and the fighting in Yemen is now hitting government forces' staging areas in the south as well as Saudi cities. Oil, for now, is ignoring it — Brent settled Friday at $95.84, down about 2.5 percent on the week, with the International Energy Agency saying supply exceeded demand for the first time since the war began.
In short: the Gulf crisis is now a UN argument, a US travel warning, and a ground war in southern Yemen at the same time — while Iran's daily mine claims remain unverified and oil prices keep falling on oversupply. Watch for any UKMTO confirmation of the latest tanker claims, and for whether the government offensive in Lahij holds.
Sources:
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: Nvidia's board has approached Arm's CEO about the top job, FT reports
item.description:
Nvidia's board has approached Arm Holdings chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported on Friday. There is no guarantee he will be offered the job or would accept it, and the board said it was in the process of selecting an executive search firm and had not formally engaged any potential candidates. Colette Kress remains interim CEO while also serving as CFO, and longtime board member Harvey Jones has taken over as chairman. Other names floated by industry watchers include AMD chief Lisa Su, Micron chief Sanjay Mehrotra, Marvell chief Matt Murphy and Apple's hardware chief Johny Srouji — and President Trump has publicly pushed former Apple CEO Tim Cook. Earnings are Tuesday, November 17, Kress's first call as interim chief. Why it matters: Nvidia is the world's most important AI chip company and its stock is down more than 30 percent since early October; who runs it decides how the export-control fight around its China sales plays out.
Sources:
Source: probespakistan.com.

item.title: OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet — its AI agents can now shop for you
item.description:
OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet on Friday, November 13, a payment feature letting its autonomous AI agents, called dots, make purchases for users. The launch was carried by nine outlets in Friday's AI news roundup. Why it matters: it is the first time a mainstream chatbot can complete purchases on its own — the agentic-commerce idea moving from demo to a real product, with all the fraud and mistaken-order questions that come with it.
Sources:
Source: theworldofai.org.

item.title: SilentAir hijacks Asian telecom nodes to intercept SMS 2FA codes
item.description:
Telecom security firm Enea disclosed on November 11 that a state-level cyberespionage actor it calls SilentAir has been using compromised equipment inside mobile operators in at least six Asian countries to intercept the calls and text messages of selected subscribers — mainly in Taiwan, including political and government figures — and to harvest incoming SMS two-factor authentication codes. The group sends forged SS7 and Diameter location-update messages into the shared IPX interconnect network, telling the target's home network that the attacker's node now serves the target's phone, so inbound calls and SMS get rerouted through it. Enea observed 2FA codes being intercepted immediately after some diversions took effect, pointing to attempts to access accounts registered to the same phone number — though it did not establish whether any account takeover succeeded. Interception made up 18.3 percent of SilentAir's observed activity, versus 2.1 percent for a typical commercial surveillance firm. Enea has tracked the activity since early 2025 and assesses with high confidence that SilentAir is state-level, but with low confidence that it is China-nexus; it says the group is disrupted for now but could return, and the compromised equipment has not been confirmed cleaned up. The same Enea report documents GTPDoor v3, a Linux implant inside operator core networks that now tunnels its command-and-control through GTP-U, the mobile data protocol still used in 5G. Why it matters: there is no patch for this — the flaw is the trust model of the global signalling network itself, and SMS-based 2FA is only as safe as the carrier routing it. If you rely on SMS codes for anything important, an authenticator app or hardware key is the fix.
Sources:
Source: malaysianwireless.com.

item.title: CISA KEV deadlines land Monday
item.description:
No new additions to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog overnight. The two flaws added Friday — Check Point CVE-2026-123039 (Gaia DynamicCLI privilege escalation, exploited since late October chained with the PHP2Shell flaws, with a wiper run against VMware ESXi hosts in the Israel-focused first wave) and UnrealIRCd CVE-2026-114713 (command injection, exploitation attempts began the day after the November 7 hotfix) — both carry a federal patch deadline of Monday, November 16.
Sources:
Source: thehackernews.com.

item.title: Israel: Eisenkot rejects Netanyahu's unity offer; talks set for Sunday
item.description:
Caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu renewed his appeal on Saturday for a national unity government with Gadi Eisenkot, the rival now negotiating a coalition of his own — and Eisenkot rejected it within minutes as a political ploy. Netanyahu said a meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday had strengthened his view that Israel urgently needed a broad-based government, citing Iran as the central security challenge, and urged talks without preconditions. Eisenkot said Netanyahu's appeal was a bluff, pointing out that negotiating teams from Likud and his Yashar party had already scheduled a meeting for Sunday, November 15 — and said he would sit with Likud members if their commitment to unity was sincere, but ruled out serving in a government led by Netanyahu. Under Eisenkot's plan, his 48-lawmaker bloc would back a minority government while the 46 who support Netanyahu vote against and 26 members from Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties abstain. Lawmakers are due to elect a Knesset speaker on Tuesday, November 17; Eisenkot has nominated Matan Kahana and challenged Netanyahu to back him as a test of good faith. Why it matters: the October 27 election produced no majority, and whether a minority government relying on Arab-party abstentions can take office decides who governs Israel while the Iran standoff runs.
Sources:
Source: lapresse.us.
