item.title: Zelensky says the US floated swapping Donbas for NATO membership — as overnight strikes kill a family in Belgorod
item.description:
The US floated the idea of Ukraine ceding the eastern Donbas region to Russia in exchange for NATO membership during the recent US-brokered talks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday — the first time, he said, that such a trade has ever been put to Kyiv. The revelation landed on the same morning both countries reported fresh deadly overnight drone strikes.
According to CNN and the BBC, Zelensky told journalists that American negotiators raised the question during the talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week: "What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" He called it "the first time this had been raised." US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff had shuttled from Moscow — where they met Vladimir Putin on Thursday — to Dublin to meet Zelensky, and the Abu Dhabi sessions on Tuesday and Wednesday were described as constructive by both Zelensky and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, though they ended without a breakthrough. The Kyiv Independent, cited by several outlets, reports Zelensky was told Washington had sketched security guarantees modeled on NATO's Article 4 and Article 5 commitments, delivered bilaterally and more like the guarantees the US gives Israel, with no American troops stationed in Ukraine — but he stressed the details do not exist yet: "We need specifics, and we don't have them yet."
Zelensky was careful not to treat the idea as an offer. He said Ukraine would not give up territory, and that if he received a "comprehensive security package" — a strong Ukrainian army, guarantees from NATO, money to rebuild — he would put it to the public: "If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not? I have no right to make that decision on my own." He also insisted any deal could not recognize occupied areas as Russian. US officials had previously said Ukrainian NATO membership was off the table; Zelensky said the exchange made him believe "NATO is back on the agenda." No confirmation from Washington of Zelensky's account has been reported, and it is not known who on the American side raised it.
The two sides are far apart on both halves of the proposed bargain. Moscow has long demanded all of Donbas, including the slice Ukraine still holds, and has cited NATO membership as a reason for the invasion in the first place. A list of Russia's demands obtained by Bild and reported by Politico — including keeping occupied land and gaining more, demilitarizing Ukraine's ports, and removing NATO bases from the Baltic states — was already partly reported on Friday; the Bild list adds the ports demand. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has rejected renegotiating the European security architecture ("There is one" — NATO), and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned against walking into Russia's traps, insisting on a ceasefire first. And NATO membership is not Washington's to give: it needs the unanimous agreement of all 32 allies, 30 of them European.
Meanwhile the war went on overnight. Russia's Defense Ministry said it intercepted 29 Ukrainian drones overnight, including several over the Moscow region. A drone hit a private house in Proletarsky, in the Belgorod region about 20km from the Ukrainian border, killing a married couple and their daughter — reports differ on the daughter's age, with the regional headquarters saying 24 years old and Al Jazeera reporting 24 months. Nine more people were injured in Belgorod. In the other direction, Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 96 drones from Friday evening, of which 81 were shot down or electronically suppressed, with hits at eight locations. A woman was killed in Yasna Polyana in the Donetsk region, three people were injured in Hlukhiv in the Sumy region, and one person was killed and two injured in the Kharkiv region. In Odesa, nearly 50,000 people lost electricity after a morning strike on a DTEK power facility, and the road across the Dnipro hydroelectric dam in Zaporizhzhia was closed to traffic on Saturday morning. Russia's Defense Ministry said its strikes hit an energy facility in the Chernihiv region and a cargo ship delivering military supplies to Odesa. Neither side's claims could be independently verified.
Separately, Finland's military detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, while the Abu Dhabi talks were under way. Ukraine's Security Service said it attacked the Buyan-M-class small missile ship Naro-Fominsk; Estonian media reported the vessel later returned to St. Petersburg. Finland said it was not under any immediate military threat. The same day, Ukrainian drones caused a fire in the Russian port area of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers — part of the Baltic spillover already reported this week.
For ordinary people, the Donbas question is the war in miniature: the towns Ukraine still holds in Donetsk are home to civilians who would be handed to Russian control under any withdrawal, and the NATO-membership half of the trade would decide whether Ukraine ever gets the guarantee it has sought since 2022 — or whether it gives up land first and waits on a promise that 32 capitals must still approve. On the ground, the overnight toll is the familiar one: families killed in their homes, tens of thousands without power as winter approaches, and energy infrastructure hit on both sides.
In short: Zelensky says Washington has, for the first time, raised trading Donbas for NATO membership — a question, not a deal, with no US confirmation and no specifics yet, and with Moscow's demands running in the opposite direction. Watch whether Washington confirms the account, and whether the idea survives contact with Moscow or with Ukraine's own public. The next diplomatic date is the November 19 trilateral in Shenzhen, which pointedly excludes Ukraine.
Sources:
Source: cnn.com.

item.title: Iran claims four more tanker mine strikes in about a day — none verified, and oil fell anyway
item.description:
Iran's military claimed another round of tanker explosions in the Strait of Hormuz overnight, the fourth mine-strike claim in about a day — but as with every claim in this run, no vessel has been named, no flag or crew reported, and no maritime authority has confirmed any of them.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said on Friday night that two oil tankers, including a supertanker, had exploded and caught fire after hitting naval mines while trying to cross the strait by what it called an "unauthorized" route, with their radar and navigation systems switched off. Iran's conventional navy then said on Saturday morning that another tanker had caught fire after hitting a mine east of the strait. That follows Friday's claim of a gas carrier hitting a mine, and a run of similar claims since October 17 — two tankers on November 1, more on November 11 and 12 — all unverified. Reuters reported it could not immediately verify the latest reports.
The gap between Iran's claims and the incident record keeps widening. The UK Maritime Trade Operations center had logged 163 conflict-related maritime incidents since February 28 as of its November 13 weekly report, 141 of them involving damage to a vessel, while the International Maritime Organization had verified at least 130 attacks on commercial vessels, in which 25 seafarers have died and at least three ships have sunk. UKMTO has confirmed only a handful of the incidents Iran has claimed in the past week. US Central Command has repeatedly called Iran's reports false and says the main transit routes remain cleared of mines.
The two sides tell different stories about why this is happening. Tehran says it is asserting control over the strait and escalating attacks on ships it considers unauthorized, in response to the US naval blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions. Washington's line is that the claims are fabricated, the routes are clear, and US escorts continue — and that the blockade, not new strikes, is the pressure that works. The diplomacy is frozen: Iran's seven-day roadmap (blockade lifted, sanctions waived, ~$12bn in frozen assets released, Hormuz reopened on day 6) was rejected by Trump, who said this week "we don't need a deal with Iran."
For everyone else, the market is telling a different story than the headlines. Brent crude settled Friday at $95.84 a barrel, up two cents, and WTI at $88.56 — both down about 2.5 percent for the week, a second straight weekly loss. The International Energy Agency said Friday that global supply exceeded demand for the first time since the war began, with the market expected to return to surplus in the fourth quarter, and US crude output hit a record 14.013 million barrels a day in the week ending November 6. Traders are pricing in the blockade and the surplus, not the mine claims — but shipping through the strait is still running roughly 65 percent below pre-conflict volume, and the cost of moving oil around the Gulf keeps climbing.
In short: Iran claimed four tanker mine strikes in about a day, none independently confirmed, while the verified count stands at 163 incidents since February with 25 seafarers dead. Oil ended the week down anyway on a growing supply surplus. Watch for any UKMTO confirmation of the latest incidents — that, not another Iranian claim, is what would move prices and policy.
Sources:
Source: jbiznews.com.

item.title: Reuters: Huang misled Nvidia's top lawyer about the Megaspeed affair
item.description:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang misled several of the company's leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld, about the nature of his relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, according to two people familiar with the matter and internal correspondence reviewed by Reuters. It is the first reporting on the correspondence, and it deepens the scandal that forced Huang's resignation on Thursday.
Reuters reviewed several exchanges from October, on condition of not quoting verbatim. In two separate messages that month, Huang told Nvidia leaders, including Teter and Wagonfeld, that his interactions with Alice Huang and her company Megaspeed reflected "standard business dealings with customers." In other messages he affirmed the routine nature of the interactions. He had given similar assurances in autumn 2025 after press queries drew leaders' attention to the relationship. Huang also discussed taking legal action against the New York Times after it published an article in October 2025 drawing attention to his public meetings with Alice Huang; no lawsuit was ever filed. Reuters verified photos of the two together in the US, China and elsewhere dating as far back as December 2023. It is unclear when the relationship became intimate. Teter did not respond to Reuters' request for comment, Wagonfeld did not immediately respond, and a representative for Huang and an Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment.
Alice Huang is a former top executive of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm and Nvidia business partner in the Asia-Pacific region; she became its controlling shareholder in March 2023, according to the research group C4ADS. The New York Times reported in October 2025 that Megaspeed was under US investigation over whether it helped Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to export controls; there has been no public finding that it violated the rules, and Megaspeed says it has cooperated with US inspections. The Times also reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a classified memo in spring 2026 detailing intelligence indicating China's Ministry of State Security had recruited Alice Huang to target Nvidia's CEO, and that Rubio briefed President Trump about it aboard Air Force One in May. Reuters says it has not independently verified whether Alice Huang was working for the Chinese government, and Beijing has denied she is a spy. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on November 12 that the Justice Department had not yet reached a conclusion on whether she was a spy. The Times reported earlier this week that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia employee, and Reuters reported Thursday that he had another intimate relationship with a different Nvidia employee.
The political fallout is widening beyond the boardroom. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that his department had favored putting Megaspeed on the US entity list for months, but that it was up to the Commerce Department to act. "The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" Bessent told CNBC. Lawmakers have called for tougher restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips, and the scandal has drawn in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whom Axios reported had stalled a crackdown on suspected Nvidia chip diverters. The Information reported that Huang's ties to Alice Huang facilitated at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip sales to China. Nvidia's board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz on November 10 to run an independent investigation.
Huang's side has said little. He apologized in a statement on Sunday for being unfaithful to his wife and for disappointing the company, without naming Alice Huang, and said in a Bloomberg interview published October 29 that the US government had not informed him about its suspicions regarding her. The board's investigation continues, Congress is preparing a probe, and interim CEO Colette Kress faces her first earnings call on Tuesday, November 17.
For ordinary people, the stakes are in their portfolios and in the AI economy: Nvidia's stock has fallen more than 30 percent since its October 6 closing high of $239.24, erasing more than $1.8 trillion in market value, and the affair has turned the question of who gets America's most advanced AI chips — and how they are policed — into a Washington fight. What began as a personal scandal is now a test of whether the export-control system around the world's most important chip company actually works.
In short: Reuters reports Huang told Nvidia's own general counsel and marketing chief his dealings with Alice Huang were routine business, in messages reviewed by the outlet — the first direct evidence he misled the company's leadership. The spying allegations against her remain unverified, the DOJ has reached no conclusion, and Treasury wanted Megaspeed blacklisted months ago. Watch Tuesday's earnings call, the board's investigation, and whether Commerce finally puts Megaspeed on the entity list.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: The FAA grounded every departing flight in America on Friday
item.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, halting departures at every US airport — the first nationwide stop since January 2023 and only the second since the September 11 attacks. It was lifted Friday night, but the disruption is expected to linger for days.
The FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center issued the order at 3:54 p.m. ET, "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety," after a telecommunications outage hit the Air Route Traffic Control Centers that manage high-altitude en-route traffic across the country. "There has been a temporary telecommunications outage — out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis," the agency said. More than 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the stop was issued; Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said they were all coordinated to safe landings, with fewer than 400 still in the air by the time of his briefing. FlightAware counted roughly 7,000 flights delayed or cancelled, and other tallies put the total affected above 10,000. The ground stop was lifted at about 8:19 p.m. ET, and the FAA said Saturday morning that air traffic operations had returned to normal — while warning that it will take time to resume normal operations and passengers should keep checking with their airlines.
The cause is still being pinned down, and the accounts differ on the details. CBS News reported the outage was caused by a failed update to the L3Harris-operated communications system connecting air traffic control centers, which forced a reboot and then crashed. The FBI does not believe the outage was a cyberattack or criminality, according to a person familiar with the matter, and a software update is one area of inquiry. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no indication the stop was due to a threat. Duffy blamed aging infrastructure: the system still runs on analog TDM telecom, he said, and he is seeking an additional $30 billion from Congress for the air traffic control overhaul on top of the $12.5 billion obtained in 2025. The disruption began at about 3:36 p.m., when radar and communications at control centers and TRACON facilities nationwide became unstable.
The timing could hardly be worse. Thanksgiving is November 26, less than two weeks away, and the system was already strained: about 28,852 flights were scheduled to leave US airports on Friday, carrying 3.54 million seats, roughly 90 percent of them domestic. Airline stocks fell after the close — JetBlue down 3.5 percent, Delta 1.3 percent, American 1.7 percent, United 1.5 percent. The stop also coincided with a widespread Microsoft 365 outage affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot, though there is no indication the two incidents are related.
For travelers, the practical effect is a weekend of rebookings and ripple delays: the FAA itself says normal operations will take time to resume, and with the holiday travel peak approaching, a system that can be brought down nationwide by a single telecom failure is now a political question as much as a technical one. Duffy is using the outage to press Congress for the extra $30 billion; critics will ask why $12.5 billion in overhaul funding did not prevent it.
In short: a telecom outage knocked out communications at every en-route air traffic control center on Friday afternoon, grounding all US departures for about four and a half hours in the first nationwide stop since January 2023. It was not a cyberattack, per the FBI, and flights are moving again — but delays will linger, and the failure has put the FAA's aging systems back at the center of a funding fight days before Thanksgiving.

Source: thehindubusinessline.com.

item.title: Houthis claim fresh strikes on Riyadh airport and pipeline pumping station — still unconfirmed
item.description:
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said Friday that one drone targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and two drones struck Pumping Station No. 3 on the East-West oil pipeline east of the capital, and that two ballistic missiles hit gatherings of Saudi forces in Al-Tuwal in Jazan, claiming dozens killed or wounded including Sudanese nationals.
He described the round as the 24th operation in about three days. No Saudi confirmation as of Saturday morning, and no photos or other evidence of damage were published.
The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday it had intercepted two Houthi drones, one in the Riyadh region and one in the Eastern Province. Yemen's internationally recognized government condemned the attacks on Friday, including launches toward Mecca, calling them a violation of Saudi sovereignty.
Why it matters: the claims keep coming daily and the Houthis say the campaign is escalating — but with no Saudi confirmation, treat them as claims, not confirmed hits. Sources:
Source: sambadenglish.com.

item.title: Google makes Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default in Search
item.description:
Google has rolled out Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Search globally and for all users, making it the default model in AI Mode, days after releasing it as a coding and agents model.
Google calls it the largest single change to its search engine's model, with better handling of complex or misspelled questions, broader link surfacing and richer visual answers. This follows the Gemini 4 Argon release last month.
Why it matters: the fast, cheap model is now what every Google searcher gets, not just developers. Source:
Source: ppc.land.

item.title: SCKit fallout: Microsoft publishes the full attack chain, five ScreenConnect extensions disabled
item.description:
Microsoft's Security Blog published a detailed analysis of SCKit on Friday: the worm abuses cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to install rogue clients, decrypts and extracts the toolkit with device-specific key material, establishes persistence through scheduled tasks and registry Run entries, and deploys a component called RelayTrap designed to deliver a payload to a connecting technician's workstation — spreading from a customer's device up to the technician and onward into other managed networks.
ConnectWise disabled five third-party ScreenConnect extensions across roughly 400 partner environments, and Huntress found unauthorized sessions on more than 100 ScreenConnect servers disguised with crypto-exchange names, apparently as bait for technicians. The initial access route is still unidentified; the RMM+ extension (versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32), which accepted a blank access key when none was configured, is the leading suspect, and Huntress says it has not observed the previously patched CVE-2026-84869 being exploited in this campaign.
Patch ScreenConnect to 26.6.5 or later. Why it matters: this is the second remote-management tool hit in a week, and the entry point is still unknown — MSPs should treat any ScreenConnect session as untrusted until the investigation closes.
Sources:
Source: microsoft.com.

item.title: Baker Tilly discloses third-party breach affecting nearly 196,000 people
item.description:
Accounting firm Baker Tilly disclosed that an unauthorized party took clients' and their dependents' personal data, including Social Security numbers, from a third-party platform it uses for client services.
The breach was discovered on September 6, 2026; a Texas filing lists 10,456 residents and 195,512 affected nationwide. Why it matters: another breach that started outside the victim's own perimeter — the third-party platform, not Baker Tilly's systems, was the entry point.

item.title: Open source
item.description:
GitHub trending for Saturday, November 14 is led by a new #1: alibaba/open-code-review (~50.7k stars) — an AI code review CLI with deterministic pipelines and an LLM agent, built from Alibaba's internal assistant; it reads git diffs and writes line-level comments.
Other names rising today: GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src (+1.9k/day) — the source repo of modern web guidance for coding agents; openai/codex-security (13.2k, +751/day) — CLI and SDK to find and fix code vulnerabilities; we-promise/sure (14.8k, +925/day) — a self-hosted personal finance app, a community fork of Maybe Finance; Likely7/Veyra-NRVideo (+256/day) — a Windows video player with real-time GPU enhancement, DLSS 5 and frame generation; ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp — Chrome DevTools for coding agents through MCP and a CLI; tailcat — netcat over Tailscale's encrypted data plane; buzz — a shared workspace where humans and AI agents share rooms; backnotprop/plannotator — a local, browser-based review surface for coding agents; and ZhuLinsen/daily_stock_analysis — LLM-based multi-market stock analysis with automated alerts. New smaller names: libracoder/kiri (+585/day) — a small, fast container runtime for macOS, Windows and Linux; expo/exact (+583/day) — write an app once, run natively on web, macOS, iOS and Linux, with an AI agent able to build, run and test it on every platform.

item.title: Murdaugh: Friday hearing argued, no ruling — written order due by November 20
item.description:
Alex Murdaugh's lawyers spent nearly two hours Friday arguing that lead SLED investigator David Owen misled the July 2022 grand jury — defense attorney Jim Griffin called the testimony "made from whole cloth" — and asking Judge Debra McCaslin to throw out all four indictments (two murder, two weapons).
Prosecutor Creighton Waters pushed back, saying the disputed statements were mistakes or imprecise descriptions rather than intentional deception, and that other evidence supported the indictments. McCaslin took the motion under advisement and will issue a written order by Friday, November 20.
She asked Waters whether the state could re-indict by December 10 and still keep the April 5, 2027 trial date; the defense said it would not oppose re-indictment. Even if the motion is granted, the retrial is expected to proceed.
Sources:
Source: greenvilleonline.com.

item.title: Trump, Putin and Xi to meet face-to-face for the first time — but Ukraine is off the agenda
item.description:
The White House confirmed Friday that President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping will hold the first-ever three-way meeting of the leaders of the United States, Russia and China on Thursday, November 19, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. The stated agenda is cutting nuclear weapons and the war in Iran. Ukraine, notably, is not on it.
The meeting, announced by White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales, will bring together the leaders of the world's three biggest nuclear powers. According to Reuters, Trump leaves Washington on Monday for a four-day Asia trip — the Philippines first for the ASEAN summit, then Shenzhen for APEC, which runs November 18–19. He will also hold a separate bilateral working lunch with Xi on Thursday, but no one-on-one with Putin is scheduled. Elon Musk is expected to travel with Trump, though he is not expected to attend the trilateral session.
The arms-control backdrop is stark. The last nuclear arms treaty between the U.S. and Russia expired in February, leaving the two largest atomic arsenals uncapped for the first time in more than half a century, while China has been rapidly building up its own stockpile. The White House says Trump will push for reductions, and the meeting is billed as the start of a process rather than a deal-making session — a senior U.S. official told reporters, "We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement." China has never been party to a U.S.-Russia arms treaty, and analysts quoted by Reuters note Beijing is hesitant to engage on disarmament because it holds far fewer weapons than the other two.
The Iran war is also on the agenda, according to U.S. officials. No ceasefire has been in force since one collapsed in early July, and the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports remains in place. Ukraine, by contrast, was deliberately left out. "China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," one U.S. official said, referring to the separate U.S.-led negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow. Trump is also not expected to raise Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starlink/StarShield service, which has been a running sore in U.S.-Ukraine relations this week.
Reactions split along familiar lines. The White House frames the gathering as historic diplomacy — three nuclear powers talking directly about reducing arsenals. Analysts are far more cautious: Hoo Tiang Boon of Nanyang Technological University told Reuters the meeting could undercut China's effort at APEC to present itself as a defender of free trade, while other analysts say it may overshadow the summit itself. Critics, including voices quoted by Political.org, warn the format risks legitimizing Putin while the Ukraine war continues and sidelines Kyiv and European allies. For Moscow, the meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing; for Beijing, hosting it is a showcase of growing clout. Xi and Putin have met more than 40 times since 2013; Trump and Putin seven times, most recently in Alaska in August 2025.
For ordinary people, the stakes are real even if no deal emerges Thursday. With the last U.S.-Russia treaty gone, there are currently no caps on the world's two biggest nuclear arsenals — the guardrails that defined the last half-century of arms control are simply absent. Any discussion of the Iran war at the same table also feeds directly into oil prices and shipping costs, which have already been climbing through the autumn. And for Ukrainians, the exclusion stings: the war heads into its fifth winter, and Kyiv and European capitals fear decisions about their future being signaled in rooms they are not in. Former U.S. official Edgard Kagan put it bluntly — the key for Putin is signaling that leaders are making decisions on Ukraine in a way Ukrainians and Europeans do not like.
In short: a first-of-its-kind Trump–Putin–Xi sit-down is set for Thursday in Shenzhen, focused on nuclear arms cuts and Iran, with Ukraine explicitly off the agenda and officials themselves warning not to expect an agreement. Watch whether any joint statement or framework emerges, and whether China signals any willingness to join arms limits it has always avoided.
Sources:
Source: kz1023.com.

In short: a first-of-its-kind Trump–Putin–Xi sit-down is set for Thursday in Shenzhen, focused on nuclear arms cuts and Iran, with Ukraine explicitly off the agenda and officials themselves warning not to expect an agreement. Watch whether any joint statement or framework emerges, and whether China signals any willingness to join arms limits it has always avoided.

item.title: Iran threatens "unlimited response" after a day of claims and counter-claims in the Gulf
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard raised the temperature again on Friday, declaring its Aerospace Force on "full alert to respond without limits" to any further aggression in the Strait of Hormuz — the sharpest operational threat from Tehran since Supreme Leader Khamenei's October 31 order to senior commanders. The warning followed a day in which both sides claimed victories the other denies, and a gas carrier reportedly hit a mine and exploded in the strait.
The trigger, according to Iran, was a strike on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, a port city on the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state media said the tower was hit by "enemy fire" but named no attacker; U.S. Central Command has not publicly acknowledged any strike on Sirik. The IRGC says it retaliated by targeting a U.S. early-warning radar at Jabal ad Dukhan in Bahrain. CENTCOM says the reality was different: two Iranian one-way attack drones were launched toward Bahrain and both were shot down by U.S. forces, with no injuries and no damage — and it called the radar-destruction claim false. Bahrain's government had not confirmed any attack on the radar as of Friday evening. No independent third party has verified either account, and the IRGC released no imagery or coordinates for the claimed hit.
Iranian state media piled on further claims on Friday: the IRGC Navy said a liquefied petroleum gas carrier struck a naval mine and exploded while transiting the eastern Strait of Hormuz, after ignoring warnings to stay off an unauthorized route. The Associated Press reports that claim could not be independently verified and there was no immediate report of the incident from UKMTO, the British military agency that monitors incidents at sea. Tehran's hardline Kayhan newspaper added that Iranian forces downed a U.S. MQ-1 Predator drone near Kuhestak in southern Iran — also unverified, with no U.S. confirmation. The IRGC's commander-in-chief, Ahmad Vahidi, separately warned that "the slightest aggression" would draw "devastating and painful strikes."
The numbers behind the standoff keep climbing. The Joint Maritime Information Center counted 181 confirmed maritime incidents since March 1, including four in its latest reporting window, and rates the threat level in the strait as severe, with deliberate attacks highly likely. UKMTO's weekly report through November 10 put commercial transits roughly 65 percent below pre-conflict levels. U.S.-facilitated transits totaled 135 between November 8 and 11, against a historical average of about 138 vessels a day. Lloyd's List, cited in earlier reporting, counted 37 vessel attacks in October — a record monthly total — with more than 14 already in November.
The two sides are telling very different stories about where this is heading. Tehran frames its actions as defensive retaliation for attacks on its own infrastructure, and insists the radar strike was a "serious warning" to stop aerial provocations. Washington's line, via CENTCOM, is that the drones were intercepted, nothing was hit, and the ceasefire Trump described earlier this week remains in effect. The broader context cuts against calm: Trump declared this week that "we don't need a deal with Iran" and pulled Vice President Vance off the negotiations file, while a third U.S. carrier strike group is en route to the region and Iran has unveiled an underground missile production site.
For people in the region, the practical effects are already visible: shipping through the world's most important oil chokepoint is running at about a third of normal volume, which is what keeps oil prices elevated and pushes up fuel and transport costs far beyond the Gulf. U.S. personnel at Naval Support Activity Bahrain — headquarters of the Fifth Fleet — are the direct target of these drone launches, and the U.S. has already issued a rare coordinated security alert for citizens across 12 Middle Eastern countries. Gulf carriers and insurers are pricing in a strait that could shut with little notice.
In short: Friday brought a new round of unverified Iranian claims — a destroyed U.S. radar, a downed Predator drone, a mined gas carrier — all denied or unconfirmed by the U.S., plus Tehran's bluntest threat yet of an "unlimited response." Nothing has been independently confirmed, but with shipping already down 65 percent and 181 maritime incidents since March, the Gulf is one miscalculation away from a much worse week. Watch for any UKMTO confirmation of the gas carrier incident and whether the U.S. responds publicly to the Sirik strike.
Sources:
Source: houseofsaud.com.

item.title: Houthis say they fired missiles at Saudi forces in Jazan
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis said Friday they fired two ballistic missiles at what they described as concentrations of Saudi forces in Al-Tuwal in Jazan province, hours after Saudi civil defence issued an all-clear for the province.
The group also claimed it attacked Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of any of the claims.
Jazan is home to a Saudi Aramco refinery with a capacity of 400,000 barrels of crude a day, and southern Saudi Arabia has been hit repeatedly in recent weeks. Why it matters: the claims, if real, would show the Houthis still reaching deep into Saudi territory despite weeks of coalition strikes — but with no Saudi confirmation, treat them as claims, not confirmed hits.
Source:
Source: froggyweb.com.

item.title: Ukraine: no new verified overnight barrage by 10 PM CT
item.description:
No new verified overnight attacks on either side had been reported by brief time.
The last confirmed exchange remains Thursday night into Friday: Ukraine's ~1,200-drone barrage (including the confirmed Volgograd Lukoil refinery hit) and Russia's 117 drones at Ukraine. One sketchy mirror site claimed a fresh Kyiv clinic strike overnight; with no corroboration from any established outlet, it is not reported here as fact.
The diplomatic track to watch is now the November 19 trilateral in Shenzhen — which pointedly excludes Ukraine — alongside the U.S.-led talks with Kyiv and Moscow.

item.title: SCKit worm rides ScreenConnect into MSPs — 288 computers, 48 organizations
item.description:
A worm-like toolkit called SCKit has been spreading through rogue ScreenConnect clients, hitting at least 288 computers across 48 organizations since November 11.
Attackers used cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push commands that installed attacker-controlled clients, built to spread from a customer's device up the support session to the technician's machine and onward into other managed networks. Huntress, which spotted the campaign, says the malware tries to exploit CVE-2026-84869 during support sessions.
ConnectWise says the access came through abuse of a third-party extension that bypassed authentication. Patch ScreenConnect to version 26.6.5 or later.
Why it matters: this is the second remote-management tool hit this week — N-central was compromised the same way, hours after a public exploit — and MSPs are the soft underbelly because one technician's machine can open dozens of client networks. Sources:
Source: feed.anmolsinghyadav.com.

item.title: FBI and DOJ take down North Korea's FaceStealer crypto scheme — $400M+ stolen via fake video calls
item.description:
North Korean actors operating as Sapphire Sleet / BlueNoroff / APT38 stole more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over 18 months by hijacking Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord accounts and inviting targets to video meetings on typosquatted fake Zoom or Teams sites, replaying stolen webcam video to impersonate real people.
The FBI issued a FLASH alert and the Justice Department seized the scheme's cloud infrastructure, along with more than $1.2 billion tied to the Binance theft attributed to TraderTraitor, and over 900 victim videos. Why it matters: it is one of the largest crypto-theft takedowns ever, and the social-engineering trick — a "colleague" on a video call who is not who they seem — works on anyone, not just crypto firms.
Sources:
Source: ninjalabz.io.

item.title: Europol's Operation Endgame seizes Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC infrastructure
item.description:
Europol and partners from nine countries seized hundreds of servers and domains behind the Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC operations.
The DOJ cited at least 44 U.S. Gootloader ransomware victims. German investigators traced the rebuilt StealC network to a bulletproof hosting provider the FBI seized in October.
Why it matters: StealC has now been taken down twice in one year — expect the stealer crews to rebuild again, so refresh blocklists rather than trusting last month's. Source:
Source: ninjalabz.io.

item.title: Check Point attack follow-up: wiper hit VMware hosts in Israel-focused first wave
item.description:
New detail on the Check Point gateway attacks added to CISA's KEV catalog on Thursday: in the first wave from October 30, aimed mostly at Israeli organizations, attackers ran a wiper called destroy_v6 on VMware ESXi hosts after gaining root via the PHP2Shell + CVE-2026-123039 chain.
The wiper note is in Hebrew and politically themed, rejecting any ransom negotiation. A second, wider wave from November 2 hit several countries and sectors with no destructive activity seen so far.
Check Point says a couple of dozen gateways were compromised. The fix is the November Jumbo Hotfix.
Source:
Source: reef-sentinel.net.

item.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster, cheaper model for coding and agents
item.description:
Google has released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster and lower-cost model built for coding and AI agents, available through Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Search and the Gemini app.
Google says it runs about 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash and scores strongly on coding tests, at $1.50 per million input tokens. This follows the Gemini 4 Argon release last month.
Why it matters: Google is now shipping a new Gemini 4 variant roughly monthly, and the pricing undercuts most rivals for agent workloads. Sources:
Source: theneuron.ai.

item.title: Nvidia shares slide overnight as leadership turmoil continues
item.description:
Nvidia shares plunged more than 8 percent in extended trading overnight after falling 4.34 percent in Thursday's regular session, following CEO Jensen Huang's resignation.
Apple and Alphabet shares edged higher in the same overnight session, with retail investors talking up a rotation out of Nvidia into more traditional tech. Nvidia's board search for a permanent successor continues, Congress is preparing a probe of the spy allegations, and earnings land Tuesday, November 17 — interim CEO Colette Kress's first call.
A rumor floated Friday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook could be a successor candidate; that is unconfirmed market chatter, not a report. Source:
Source: summamoney.com.

item.title: Open source
item.description:
GitHub trending for November 13 is mostly the same names as the evening brief — Meta's Astryx design system still #1 (~26.7k stars, +1.8k/day), craft-anything at ~31.3k, REA at ~457k, OpenAI's codex-security at ~13.2k (+751/day).
New names on the board: pingdotgg/t3code (~59k stars) — one control surface for the coding agents already on your machine, from any computer or phone; janestreet/agent_skills — Jane Street's skills that teach your agent to tutor you, Socratic style; vercel-labs/ui — keyboard, focus, popups and ARIA as a behavior library your agent can build with; and CopilotKit/OpenBot — modular AI coworkers that each get their own computer with a browser, files and tools. Google's elephant-goldfish-model (open-source plugin for designing and reviewing software with agents) is also climbing at ~18k stars.
Sources:
Source: ghtrends.dev.
